It says he later tried to buy the handle directly, presenting an esports and FPS gaming project in February 2025. That’s X’s description of the discussions and their purpose. [Paragraphs 41–43.]

Paragraph 43 names two different payers: according to X, Moonrail paid for @duel_temp’s Premium subscription, while Immortal Snail paid for @duel itself. The person negotiating, the subscription payer and the handle buyer have different roles in that account. We don’t have the full negotiation or complete banking records in this package.

The acquisition documents total $480,000:

A $300,000 invoice for @Duel, dated March 24, 2025.
An $80,000 invoice for @Monarch, dated April 16.
A $100,000 receipt for @Castle, paid on June 3.

Snail says it paid all three. But two documents are invoices and one is a receipt, so I’m not calling them three bank payment confirmations. The @Castle receipt says “Crypto.” It gives no wallet, network, asset or transaction hash to trace. [Exhibit 25, pp. 13–15.]

A handle can move between accounts. The 2024 events and the 2025 purchases don’t establish that one person continuously owned one underlying account.

Then there’s the Grizzly section shown in the screenshot.

X describes Grizzly as a former CSGOEmpire Product Manager who fell out with Ketola. It alleges that Ketola and Snail accessed one of his accounts without authorization in February 2025, after he published internal conversations. [Paragraph 30.]

According to X, the Discord and Telegram conversations discussed accessing Israeli government email accounts and using them to ask platforms to remove competitors’ accounts, including CSGORoll. The complaint also describes discussions about wording those requests to make them look like legitimate official requests.

The original emails and their headers aren’t in the package I reviewed, and I haven’t independently verified who controlled those mailboxes. None of this establishes involvement by the Israeli government.

Paragraph 31 quotes Grizzly claiming to have more than 6.5 GB of chat exports and other evidence. In that quoted post, he said the material included plans to disclose relatives’ personal information and references to physical attacks against Stake. He also said he feared for his life and was looking for a journalist to receive the files.

The full archive isn’t here. His statement that he had it doesn’t tell us whether he delivered it to X, a journalist or an authority.

Paragraph 32 describes a video conversation between “Gr1zzly” and “Monarch,” whom X identifies as Ketola. X attributes to Monarch references to Bosnian mafia contacts, plans for kidnappings and possible murders, obtaining personal information, services involving violence and statements about mutilations.

Those are exceptionally serious allegations. I haven’t authenticated the original video, and I don’t have independent evidence establishing that the acts described were carried out. I’m reporting what X attributes to that conversation.

Paragraph 33 describes another conversation, on Telegram, about using government emails to get accounts removed, with language involving escalation and violence. Here the complaint calls the participant “Ossi” and says he is presumably Ossi Ketola. “Presumably” is in the document. It stays in this account too.

X says one of Grizzly’s accounts was taken over, had its biography changed from “Ex-CSGOEmpire” to a message saying it had been seized by @theJNSAST, then was used to promote Duel. It also cites @monarchlawyer announcing an account takeover. A username containing “lawyer” doesn’t establish that the person using it is one. [Paragraph 34.]

Korra expressly denies these events in the post being quoted. That denial belongs alongside the allegations. I also couldn’t retrieve the original links in footnotes 15–18 in readable form, so the complaint and screenshots aren’t a substitute for authenticating the underlying material.

X makes a technical claim as well. Footnote 15 says @fastschitzobear, @CSGOEmpire, @CSGOEmpireV2, @duel and @monarch used the same Known Device Token. X treats that as evidence of previous access through the same device or browser and an indication of collaboration. Paragraph 50 also refers to matches involving devices, software, identifiers, cookies and financial accounts.

The complete logs and dates needed to check that conclusion aren’t in the package. A shared device doesn’t tell us who wrote a particular message, or whether the overlap happened before or after an account takeover.

There are further allegations about accounts critical of the business.

Paragraph 35 describes a trademark complaint with allegedly manipulated documents against a former CSGOEmpire social media manager. That role shouldn’t automatically be treated as the Product Manager role attributed to Grizzly. In paragraph 52, X alleges that Isik offered in June 2025 to find insiders who would suspend accounts critical of Ketola and his companies. These remain allegations in the material reviewed.

X says it suspended @duel, @monarch and @castle, along with related accounts, around October 21, 2025. It alleges that requests impersonating a US law firm followed, as did a $300,000 offer to an employee to reactivate accounts. Exhibits 1 and 2 contain the November letters X disputes. Paragraph 56 doesn’t give the exact date of the alleged offer.

There are two different $300,000 figures here. The first is the invoiced purchase price for @Duel. The second is an alleged bribe in a later incident. They shouldn’t be merged.

Paragraph 58 describes a May 2026 request that X says impersonated the Malaysian police, followed by complaints in India. The exhibits show the request fields, but they don’t authenticate the senders. I’m leaving out the names of people who may themselves have been impersonated.

X mentions Arya A. when linking an email identifier used in requests with one in billing documents. That is X’s attribution. It doesn’t establish a company position or authorship of every communication.

Snail’s side is in the file too, and it deserves to be read.

Its arbitration claim says it paid for the handles and then lost access without an adequate explanation, harming its business, reputation and commercial expectations. It wants the accounts restored and compensation. It also raises possible interference by competitors or an X shareholder connected to competitors. The material I reviewed neither names that shareholder nor establishes that theory. [Exhibit 25, pp. 4–8.]

Snail started arbitration in April 2026. X says the relevant contracts require disputes to go to Texas courts. Mohamed F. Sweify was appointed arbitrator in July. Kaplan and Cheek attended an August preliminary hearing; X had said it wouldn’t participate and maintained that position. The arbitration order put jurisdiction first.

Snail relies on the October 2025 Marketplace terms, which include arbitration subject to US residency. How those terms apply here is a question in the case, not something this post resolves.

X’s September letter mentioned possible legal actions, including RICO. That doesn’t turn this into a filed RICO claim, a criminal prosecution or an established FBI investigation.

The federal complaint names Caitlin A. Halpern and Lauryn E. Bennett of Gibbs & Bruns, and Charles W. Fillmore of Brown Pruitt, as X’s lawyers. The public docket records the case’s reassignment to Reed O’Connor on September 30. A lawyer’s representation of a party doesn’t make them responsible for the conduct being disputed.

The older company records help explain the business relationships. They need to be read with their own limits: these are supplied historical copies, and I haven’t independently certified every file’s authenticity or confirmed its official receipt. The X lawsuit doesn’t authenticate the rest of the archive.

An August 2023 organizational chart shows Ossi owning 100% of Moonrail and Moonrail owning 100% of JHOLT. That tells us what the chart records at that time; it isn’t a current ownership certificate. [D026.]

Moonrail’s shareholders’ register goes further back. The copy marked D027 reproduces a certification dated July 29, 2024. It records Xecutive Corporate Management B.V. subscribing for all 10,000 shares on October 1, 2018, then transferring them the next day. That initial shareholding is a separate role from its later corporate administration work.

The register lists these corporate holdings from October 2, 2018, and their later transfers:

JPellikka Oy, Finland, 2881789-9: 13.65%, later recorded under Day Star Enterprises OÜ, Estonia, 14630609.
Hiirijoki & Partners Oy, Finland, 2887371-9: 12.50%, later recorded under Rotten Apples OÜ, Estonia, 14631261.
create.repeat Oy, Finland, 2662670-6: 13.65%, later recorded under Simple Holdings OÜ, Estonia, 14635334.

It dates those three transfers to December 17, 2018. It then records Ketola, who already held 44.80%, acquiring the remaining 55.20% on November 13, 2019. That remaining stake consists of the three company holdings totaling 39.80%, plus an individual holding of 15.40%.

Those entries don’t tell us the purchase price or show the payments. They also don’t make those companies current owners of Duel. [D027, pp. 3–4.]

The Estonian public register confirms the companies’ identities and gives these dates:

Day Star: registered December 21, 2018; deleted from the register August 13, 2021.
Rotten Apples: registered December 27, 2018; deleted September 8, 2021.
Simple Holdings: registered January 4, 2019; deleted November 26, 2021.

All three registration dates are later than the December 17 transfer date in Moonrail’s book. That needs an explanation from the underlying documents. I can’t resolve the legally effective transfer dates from these records or call the discrepancy proof of forgery. The public company records establish those companies’ existence; the link to Moonrail’s shares comes from the supplied shareholders’ register.

Finland’s register also shows that JPellikka Oy became Veivi Ventures Oy on January 18, 2023. A later name change doesn’t establish a present-day stake in Moonrail.

There’s more on the earlier funding in a November 14, 2025 letter addressed to the Curaçao Gaming Authority. Moonrail says its initial funding came from Ketola’s earlier business activities through Global Vault oy and the distribution of that company’s assets after liquidation.

Global Vault’s Finnish registration number is 2793380-4. It was registered on November 9, 2016, and dissolved on April 1, 2019. The register confirms those facts. The explanation connecting its funds to Moonrail comes from Moonrail’s letter; it isn’t bank verification and doesn’t establish that Global Vault operated CSGOEmpire. [D050, pp. 1–3.]

The historical PRH/Virre extract issued on August 14, 2026 lists Ossi Eemeli Ketola as Global Vault’s board member and managing director from November 9, 2016 to July 5, 2018. It lists Satu Maarit Ketola as a deputy board member over the same period, and Lari Hiirijoki as a procurist, meaning a holder of a commercial power of attorney, from November 2017. His later appointment as liquidator was registered on July 5, 2018.

Those are documented business roles. They don’t establish family relationships or positions for those other individuals at today’s operators. [Global Vault PRH/Virre extract, pp. 1–3.]

The January 18, 2019 liquidator’s report in D050 identifies Ketola as holding all 100 shares and the rights to Global Vault’s asset distribution. Lari Hiirijoki signs as liquidator. This adds to the ownership and funding history, but it still doesn’t supply the records of transfers between the people and companies involved. [D050, pp. 10–11.]

There’s a one-year difference between two documents that I’m keeping visible. Moonrail’s November 2025 letter says Ketola owned 100% of Moonrail from November 13, 2018. The shareholders’ register puts his purchase of the final 55.20% on November 13, 2019. I don’t have enough to settle which date is correct.

The same letter gives Moonrail’s licensing account: Cyberluck N.V. in 2018, Antillephone N.V. in 2021, then the Gaming Control Board/Curaçao Gaming Authority framework. That is Moonrail’s account of its sublicensing and licensing history. It doesn’t establish permission to operate everywhere, and it can’t simply be applied to Immortal Snail. [D050, p. 1.]

The February 2025 assessment in the archive identifies missing documentation and recommends conditions covering management identification, anti-money-laundering measures, responsible gambling, territorial access and media policy. These are recommendations, not a sanction or proof that every proposed condition was imposed. [D029.]

A later business plan, identified in the archive as October 30, 2025, names Irene Rosenblatt as CEO, Matt Tanner as CFO and Sampsa Saarela as CTO. It names Rokas Daugirdas as compliance manager and Pearl Reiph as MLRO, the money-laundering reporting role. Xecutive is described as the board, with the CEO responsible for daily operations and reporting to it. Those are the roles this historical plan gives them. I haven’t verified that they still hold them, and the titles don’t prove involvement in X’s allegations. [D041, pp. 1–2 and 4–5.]

Moonrail’s advertising policy is worth reading in full as well. Version 1.0, dated May 29, 2025, requires prior advertising review, influencer agreements, sponsorship disclosure and territorial controls. It prohibits presenting gambling as a solution to financial difficulties, associating it with violence or dangerous behavior, and using content or influencers that appeal to minors. Advertising materials require compliance approval. Moonrail and its agents are also prohibited from offering players credit or loans to gamble. [D037, pp. 4–6.]

Those are written rules for Moonrail at that date. To assess a particular campaign against them, we’d still need to check the campaign itself, when it ran and which policy applied. Having a policy doesn’t tell us how it was followed in every case.

The archive also contains an August 1, 2025 response attributed to Xecutive on Moonrail’s behalf about Coffeezilla. It denies bribery. It says former managers proposed investigating a competitor without senior authorization, denies asking anyone to suppress or change coverage of Moonrail, and says the people who acted without authorization were removed. They aren’t named. The letter describes the owner as providing strategic guidance, separate from operational campaigns. That response needs to accompany the allegation. [D038.]

The August and November 2025 letters both present Xecutive Corporate Management B.V. as a director of Moonrail. Their signature blocks name Analissa Heiland and Lorenza Godett as its representatives. That establishes how they are presented in those letters, not participation in the alleged conduct. These letters and the other historical copies remain subject to the authenticity and date limitations explained above. [D038, p. 2; D050, p. 2.]

The regulatory decisions have their own official sources.

Spain’s decision ES/2025/011 imposes a €5 million fine and a four-year disqualification from conducting gambling activities on Moonrail for operating without the required Spanish authorization. It identifies CSGOEmpire and orders the activity to stop. The DGOJ announced the sanction in November 2025. I haven’t verified whether it was paid or the outcome of any appeals.

Sweden prohibited Moonrail from providing gambling without the required license in a decision dated November 2, 2023. Denmark’s official list includes https://t.co/wm4kIZPtIu among the domains blocked by court order in July 2023.

Those decisions apply to the countries and dates they cover. They don’t prove X’s allegations of bribery or unauthorized access. A declared Curaçao or Anjouan license doesn’t establish permission to operate in every other market either.

For people with disputes over balances or affiliate earnings, the terms themselves also matter. CSGOEmpire’s terms, marked as updated on July 7, 2026, promise withdrawals even when an account is closed and, where necessary, compensation for unclaimed referral earnings or rewards. They also contain exceptions and restrictions for abuse, self-referrals, dormant accounts and reversed trades. Any particular withholding needs to be checked against the terms that applied, the clause relied on and the account records. The page alone doesn’t prove a breach in someone’s case.

I also need to be open about my own position. I’ve filed a police complaint over a separate dispute. It records my allegations; it isn’t a judgment proving them. X’s case doesn’t settle my claims either. I’m leaving out amounts that still need reconciliation and keeping the two proceedings separate.

What we have here is a civil complaint, Snail’s arbitration claim, commercial records, a letter from lawyers describing Ketola’s ownership of both operators, historical company documents and official regulatory decisions. The most serious allegations in the complaint haven’t been established as proven in the material I’ve reviewed.

If I’ve got a document, page or date wrong, point me to it. I’ll correct it. I’ll also include responses supported by documents.

**The Unrestricted Internet Free Speech Act**  
*(The strongest practicable statutory protection of speech consistent with negative liberty and the non-aggression principle)*

**Section 1. Absolute Protection**  
Congress, the States, and every political subdivision, agency, official, or instrumentality thereof shall make no law, issue no rule, enter no order, impose no tax, license, or prior restraint, and take no action abridging the freedom of speech, of the press, or of expression on the internet or any electronic network.  

This protection is absolute as to content and viewpoint. It extends to every form of expression—words, images, video, audio, code, data, memes, satire, fiction, opinion, commercial speech, political speech, religious speech, scientific claims, false statements, offensive statements, and all other communicative acts—except only those categories that constitute initiated force or fraud under longstanding principles: true threats of imminent violence directed at a specific person, speech integral to criminal conduct (such as solicitation of a specific crime), and defamation proven by actual malice under the strictest common-law standards.

**Section 2. No Government Censorship or Compulsion**  
No public official or entity may:  
(a) remove, throttle, label, demonetize, deplatform, shadow-ban, or otherwise suppress any internet speech on the basis of its content or viewpoint;  
(b) compel any person, platform, or intermediary to speak, to host speech, to affirm any proposition, or to disclose the identity of a speaker except pursuant to a specific judicial warrant supported by probable cause of a completed crime involving force or fraud;  
(c) impose civil or criminal liability on any speaker, publisher, platform, or intermediary for the content of third-party speech;  
(d) fund, incentivize, or pressure private parties to censor speech that the government itself could not prohibit.

**Section 3. Intermediary Freedom and Immunity**  
Interactive computer services, platforms, hosts, and infrastructure providers possess the same pre-political rights of property, association, and editorial discretion as any other private owner. They may include, exclude, moderate, or refuse speech on their own property for any reason or no reason.  

They shall not be treated as publishers or speakers of third-party content and shall enjoy absolute immunity from liability arising from the speech of others or from their decisions to host or remove speech, except where they themselves originate speech that constitutes force or fraud. No law shall condition this immunity on any content-moderation practice, “neutrality” requirement, or government-approved standard.

**Section 4. Preemption and Supremacy**  
This Act preempts and supersedes any conflicting federal, state, or local statute, regulation, common-law rule, or executive action to the extent it abridges internet speech. International agreements and foreign judgments shall not be enforced within the United States if they would punish speech protected by this Act.  

Any person whose speech is abridged by government action in violation of this Act may bring suit for injunctive relief, declaratory relief, actual damages, statutory damages of not less than $100,000 per violation, and attorney’s fees. Qualified immunity is abolished for claims arising under this Act. Prevailing plaintiffs shall recover costs as of right.

**Section 5. Construction**  
This Act shall be construed in favor of maximum protection for speech and against any claimed governmental interest in suppressing expression. Ambiguities are resolved for the speaker. The internet is recognized as a domain in which the pre-political right of free speech is especially broad because exit, counter-speech, and voluntary association remain fully available.  

No emergency, public-health claim, national-security assertion, or allegation of “harm,” “misinformation,” “hate,” or “safety” shall justify any abridgment prohibited by this Act.

**Section 6. Severability and Non-Delegation**  
If any provision is held invalid, the remainder continues in force at full strength. No agency may issue rules implementing this Act that narrow its protections; any such attempt is void.

Sound the Alarm : IFF’s First Read on MeitY's Draft IT Rules Second Amendment, 2026

New Delhi, 30 March 2026

On 30 March 2026, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology published proposed amendments to the IT Rules, 2021, inviting public comments by 14 April,  a comment period of barely fifteen days for changes with far reaching consequences for free speech and intermediary governance in India. We have conducted a quick review of the draft amendments. Despite being presented as "clarificatory and procedural," they represent a dangerous expansion of executive power over online speech.

We wish to state at the outset that these proposed amendments need to be immediately withdrawn and every member in our citizenry should demand their roll back and stand with the Constitution of India. These proposed amendments come at a time of fear and increased government directed censorship, especially of online political speech that includes parody and satire of the government, including the Prime Minister.

In brief the five changes are listed below:

1. Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h): Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law.

2. Rule 3(4): Insertion of a new clause that mandates intermediary compliance with MeitY-issued clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines, making such compliance a condition for retaining safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act. These are not anchored to the rule making powers of the IT Act, 2000 and provide uncanalised power to MEITY despite it stating otherwise.

3. Rule 8(1) proviso: A substitution in the proviso that expands applicability of MIB’s oversight mechanism in Part III of the rules to:  (1) intermediaries and (2) users who are not “publishers” and post/share news and current affairs content online. This oversight mechanism contains the blocking powers of MIB by way of Rule 14 (Inter-Departmental Committee), Rule 15 (Procedure for issuing directions to block), and Rule 16 (Emergency blocking provisions).

4. Rule 14(2) : A substitution that expands the scope of the IDC from hearing "complaints or grievances" to hearing "matters", including those referred by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting.

5. Rule 14(5) : Replaces "complaints or grievances" with "the matter" in relation to IDC examination and recommendations.

A massive expansion of an unconstitutional censorship and regulatory power

First and most concerningly, Rule 3(4) creates a sweeping power for MeitY to issue binding instruments which are not anchored in law such as clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines that intermediaries must comply with as a condition of safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act.

The Supreme Court's 2015 judgment in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, remains the foundational precedent governing intermediary liability. It constrains the proposed amendments in several ways. First, the court read down Section 79(3)(b) to require that "actual knowledge" of unlawful content must come through a court order or government notification. Any Rule 3(4) making MeitY, "clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs", lower the constitutional threshold for intermediary due diligence obligations.

Further, the settled principle in Indian administrative law, reaffirmed in Indian Express Newspapers v. Union of India (1985) 1 SCC 641 and Confederation of Ex-Servicemen Associations v. Union of India (2006) 8 SCC 399, is that delegated legislation must remain within the four corners of the parent statute.  It is important to note that the rule-making power under Section 87(1) of the IT Act is confined to, "carry[ing] out the provisions" of the Act. Section 87(2)(zg) authorizes rules for intermediary guidelines under Section 79(2), and Section 87(2)(z) for blocking procedures under Section 69A(2). Justice Chandurkar's judgement in the Kunal Kamra case clearly found the FCU amendment was not properly referable to either provision. Hence, any Rule 3(4) mandating compliance with MeitY advisories would face identical challenges since they create substantive new obligations not contemplated by Sections 79 or 87.

Even though Rule 3(4)(b)(ii) states that such, “advisories” etc. need to, “clearly specify the statutory provision or legal basis under which it is issued”, since these are not required to be published or made public there is every likelihood these will be issued with secrecy and hence may just in a tautological manner refer back to Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act. This is similar to a logical fallacy in which it is clearly observable that a student is cheating on an exam who then claims that they may be permitted to continue cheating since they are stating at the same time they are not cheating. 

The practical effect of Rule 3(4) is that intermediaries face a perpetual compliance threat. Any failure to comply with any MeitY-issued instrument, however vague, however rapidly issued may cost them their safe harbour. The response for an intermediary is over-compliance and over-censorship.

Circumventing existing stay orders

The original proviso to Rule 8(1) stated that Part III applied to intermediaries only "for the purposes of rules 15 and 16"  i.e., content blocking directions and emergency blocking. The amended proviso now extends this to Rule 14, bringing intermediaries and user-generated news/current affairs content under the jurisdiction of the Inter-Departmental Committee.

Under Rules 9(1) and 9(3) of the 2021 IT Rules, there is a Code of Ethics compliance requirement and the three-tier grievance redressal mechanism, both of which were stayed by the Bombay High Court on 14 August 2021 as prima facie violative of Article 19(1)(a) and ultra vires the IT Act. On the oversight mechanism in Rules 14, 15, and 16, the Bombay High Court granted the petitioners to seek relief on this rule when an Inter Departmental Committee is established. The Madras High Court affirmed this stay as having pan-India effect in its order of 16 September 2021 in T.M. Krishna v. Union of India, observing that "an oversight mechanism to control the media by the government may rob the media of its independence." 

Both these cases, along with other cases challenging various provisions of the 2021 IT Rules, are now pending adjudication before the Delhi High Court.

The expansion of Rule 8(1) to cover Rules 14, 15, and 16 is an attempt to expand the blocking powers of MIB to both intermediaries and users who are not “publishers” but post news and current affairs content online. The IDC can now examine "matters" relating to user-generated news content on intermediary platforms without the Code of Ethics framework having been adjudicated as constitutional; the government effectively obtains the content oversight machinery that three High Courts found illegal, through a different procedural door.

Transforming the IDC from Grievance Body to Censorship Apparatus

The original Rule 14(2) required the IDC to hear "complaints regarding violation or contravention of the Code of Ethics." The amended version removes this requirement entirely. 

The IDC now hears:
(a) grievances arising from decisions at Level I or II; or
(b) "matters" referred to by the Ministry.

Clause (b) is unconstrained since, (a) there is no requirement that the "matter" arise from a complaint, (b) no requirement that the "matter" relate to a Code of Ethics violation; and (c) no requirement that the affected party be heard before the referral. The Ministry of Information and Broadcasting can, on its own motion, refer any content-related "matter" to the IDC. 

The cumulative effect of the amendments to Rules 8 and 14 is to reconstruct the oversight machinery that the Bombay and Madras High Courts found constitutionally suspect, in a form designed to evade the existing interim orders. The IDC, previously limited to the three-tier complaints process under the stayed Rules 9(3), 12, and 13 framework, now operates as a free-standing censorship committee that can take up "matters" referred by the executive.

Increased user surveillance through mandatory data retention directions

Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law. For instance, the mandatory data retention of user data beyond 180 days within Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h) may be prescribed for longer periods and other purposes raising risks of surveillance and even potentially data leaks of sensitive data that is stored for longer periods of time. Government mandates for data retention as to their legal authority and hence period of retention will be beyond those contained under the IT Act.

SOS for Digital Rights 

IFF urges an urgent rollback!

We are alarmed by the continuing expansion of unchecked executive power that is opposed to the Constitution of India. The present actions of MEITY smack of digital authoritarianism and we call on them to withdraw these proposed amendments. 

The proper course is to await judicial determination of the pending challenges, respect interim protections granted by constitutional courts, and pursue regulatory objectives through parliamentary legislation rather than subordinate instruments that exceed the parent statute.

If not withdrawn, IFF will file a detailed response before the comment deadline. We call upon all stakeholders to submit their objections before 14 April 2026 at itrules.consultation@meity.gov.in

Exemption from Liability of Intermediaries in Certain Cases

Section 79 of the Information Technology Act, 2000 provides legal protection to intermediaries against liability for third-party content hosted or transmitted through their platforms.

An intermediary includes social media platforms, internet service providers, web-hosting companies, search engines, and similar online service providers. Examples include X (Twitter), Facebook, and YouTube.

Sub-section (1)

An intermediary shall not be liable for any third-party information, data, or communication link made available or hosted by it, subject to the conditions specified in the Act.

Sub-section (2)

This protection applies only if:

The intermediary's role is limited to providing access to a communication system through which information is transmitted, temporarily stored, or hosted;

The intermediary does not initiate the transmission;

The intermediary does not select the receiver of the transmission;

The intermediary does not select or modify the information contained in the transmission; and

The intermediary observes due diligence and complies with the requirements prescribed under the Act and the applicable rules.

Sub-section (3)

The protection under Section 79 shall not apply if:

1. The intermediary has conspired, abetted, aided, or induced the commission of an unlawful act; or

2. Upon receiving actual knowledge, or upon being notified by the appropriate Government or its agency that any information, data, or communication link hosted on its computer resource is being used to commit an unlawful act, the intermediary fails to expeditiously remove or disable access to such material while preserving evidence.

Explanation

The term “Third Party Information” refers to any information dealt with by an intermediary in its capacity as an intermediary.

Practical Significance

Section 79 provides a “safe Harbour” to intermediaries. As a result, social media platforms and other intermediaries are generally not automatically liable for content posted by their users. However, if they participate in unlawful activities or fail to act after receiving a valid legal notice or government direction, they may lose the protection granted under Section 79.

The scope of this provision was further clarified by the Supreme Court of India in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India. The Court held that “Actual knowledge” for the purposes of Section 79 generally arises through a court order or a notification issued by a competent government authority, requiring the intermediary to take appropriate action.

Statement : The blocking of BitChat's code on GitHub is unconstitutional and authoritarian. 

New Delhi, 24 July 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the order issued by the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), Ministry of Home Affairs, directing GitHub to remove the code repositories of BitChat. 

The order, Notice No. 11072601011432, was issued at 11:16 pm on 23 July 2026 under Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, 2000 read with Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021. The order directs GitHub to disable access to three repositories, including the Android application and its release files, within three hours. It threatens the platform with loss of safe harbour and criminal prosecution. No copy was published by the Government of India. The public learnt of it from a post by @jack, whose team develops BitChat. Censorship in India now comes to light through disclosure by the censored.

Since 17 July 2026, the Ministry of Home Affairs has suspended mobile internet around Jantar Mantar as per public reports about five times, most recently within a 1.5 kilometre radius from 4 pm until midnight on 23 July. That radius takes in Janpath and parts of Connaught Place. Reports describe signal jammers at the protest site and people walking two kilometres before their phones work. Inside that zone a student separated from her group during a detention drive cannot send a message to say where she is. Thousands of students and young people have camped at Jantar Mantar since June, seeking accountability for examination irregularities. Permission for their march to Parliament was refused. Metro stations were shut and also internet connectivity has been blocked.

BitChat is an open source application built for exactly this situation. It passes messages from phone to phone over Bluetooth, without mobile networks or a central server. It is striking that the order does not identify a single unlawful message. It objects to what BitChat is. In its own words, the application is dangerous because it enables communication "even during network restrictions" and can "circumvent lawful restrictions" during "internet shutdowns". Hence, the government's objection is that citizens can speak to one another while it has switched the internet off. 

The order is illegal on at least four grounds. 

1. Section 79(3)(b) is not a blocking power. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court read down the provision. Intermediaries may be required to act only on a court order, or a government notification confined to the grounds under Article 19(2) of the Constitution. Blocking is governed exclusively by Section 69A and the Blocking Rules, 2009, which require a hearing and reasons recorded in writing, subject to review. Directions issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal evade these safeguards, and constitutional challenges to this parallel regime are pending before High Courts. 

2. The reasons in the order are circular. The order asserts that the repositories contain "information which is prohibited under any law" without naming any such information, and rests on what the application is "capable of" enabling. Anticipated misuse of a communications tool is not a lawful basis to prohibit the tool. By this logic a telephone exchange could be sealed. 

3. The order cites Section 43 of the IT Act, a civil compensation provision, alongside conspiracy and abetment offences under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, against a platform that hosts code. 

4. A three hour deadline issued close to midnight forecloses legal assessment and recourse, and fails the proportionality standard in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) 3 SCC 637.

The order also fails on its own terms as deleting a repository does not delete the application from any phone that carries it, and the mesh keeps functioning without servers. What the takedown actually prevents is scrutiny of the underlying code.

IFF demands that the Government of India:

1. Withdraw Notice No. 11072601011432 dated 23 July 2026 issued to GitHub.
2. Publish every takedown direction issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal, with the reasons recorded for each.
3. Restore full connectivity around Jantar Mantar, publish all suspension orders, and disclose the legal authority for the deployment of jammers.

We stand with the developers and the young protesters whose speech this order seeks to silence.

INDIA CRACKS DOWN ON AI & DEEP FAKE. BIG TECH PUT ON NOTCE

1. What has actually changed?

The Modi government amended the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 on 10 February 2026 specifically to deal with synthetically generated information and deepfakes.
The framework covers deceptive AI-generated audio, visual and audio-visual material.
The idea is no longer simply: remove illegal content after somebody complains.

Platforms are now being pushed towards:
identification
labelling
metadata
verification
automated detection
rapid takedown
and greater accountability for allowing unlawful AI content to spread.

2. AI CONTENT HAS TO BE IDENTIFIABLE
This is probably the biggest structural change.
AI-generated/synthetically altered material covered by the rules has to be clearly identifiable as synthetic.
Platforms/services enabling generation or alteration of such content must ensure appropriate labels or traceable identifiers/metadata.
The objective is simple:
REAL CONTENT ≠ AI CONTENT
The viewer should not have to conduct a forensic investigation to figure out whether something was artificially generated.
Important nuance

Don't say “every piece of text written using AI anywhere on the internet must carry a label.”

MeitY's FAQ clarifies that the operative 2026 SGI definition primarily targets audio, visual and audio-visual information, not ordinary AI-generated written text.
A more accurate line for your video is:
“India has mandated identification and labelling requirements for covered AI-generated synthetic media, particularly deepfake audio, images and video.”

3. THE BIG NUMBER: 36 HOURS → 3 HOURS

Previously, once an intermediary received legally valid knowledge of unlawful material through the prescribed government/court process, the compliance window could be 36 hours.

That has now been cut to:

3 HOURS

That is a 91.7% reduction in response time.

So something capable of going viral nationally during an election, riot, communal incident, stock-market panic or national-security crisis can no longer theoretically remain online for a day and a half after a valid takedown direction.

The platform has only hours.

4. AND SOME COMPLAINT WINDOWS ARE EVEN SHORTER

The government says timelines for grievance redressal have also been compressed.

According to the PIB explanation:
certain complaints earlier subject to 72 hours can now require action within 36 hours

particularly sensitive categories that earlier had a 24-hour timeline can now require action within 2 hours

This specifically matters for areas such as:

impersonation

intimate imagery

nudity

deepfake abuse

other highly sensitive material.

5. BIG TECH CAN'T JUST WAIT FOR A COMPLAINT

This is another major change.

The government says intermediaries must deploy reasonable and appropriate technical measures, including automated tools or other mechanisms, against unlawful synthetically generated content.
That means platforms are increasingly being pushed from:
REACTIVE MODERATION
to
PROACTIVE DETECTION
For Significant Social Media Intermediaries, the framework explicitly envisages technical measures to identify prohibited content, including certain forms of:

rape-related material

child sexual abuse material

repeat prohibited content

unlawful synthetic content.

6. USERS MAY HAVE TO DECLARE AI CONTENT

The synthetic-media framework also places responsibility upstream.

Major platforms can be required to ask users uploading covered content whether it is synthetically generated and then use technical systems to check that declaration.

So theoretically:
User uploads video →
declares AI/not AI →
platform checks →
synthetic material gets labelled.

The earlier draft framework explicitly envisaged this declaration + technical-verification model.

7. WHY THE METADATA PART MATTERS

A visible watermark can be:

cropped,
blurred,
edited,
screen-recorded,

reposted.

Metadata/identifiers create another layer of traceability.

The government's objective is therefore not merely:

“PUT AI GENERATED IN THE CAPTION.”
It is building a system where synthetic content can carry technological indicators allowing platforms to recognise what it is.
That becomes especially useful once the same manipulated video is downloaded and re-uploaded across multiple platforms.
8. THE RULES TARGET DEEPFAKE IMPERSONATION DIRECTLY
Existing IT Rules already prohibit users from publishing material that:

impersonates another person

misleads users about the origin of a message

knowingly spreads patently false or misleading information

threatens public order

violates another applicable law.

AI does not create an exemption.

If AI is being used for impersonation, fraud, defamatory fabrication or other unlawful activity, existing criminal and cyber provisions can also apply.

9. BNS CAN ALSO COME INTO PLAY
The PIB release specifically points towards provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
Depending upon what the deepfake is being used for, authorities could examine provisions relating to:
Section 319 — cheating by personation
Section 336 — forgery

Section 353 — false information/rumours capable of causing public mischief or fear

Section 111 — organised crime, where the factual circumstances justify it.

So there isn't necessarily a standalone offence called simply:

“making a deepfake.”

The legal consequence depends heavily upon what the deepfake does.

10. CHILD SEXUAL ABUSE DEEPFAKES GET SPECIAL ATTENTION
This is perhaps the least discussed but most important provision.
The amended framework explicitly covers harmful AI-generated material involving:
child sexual exploitation

non-consensual intimate imagery

impersonation

other prohibited synthetic material.

Platforms are expected to prevent such content and act rapidly when detected.

11. SOCIAL-MEDIA GIANTS HAVE EXTRA DUTIES

Platforms classified as Significant Social Media Intermediaries, broadly those crossing the prescribed Indian user threshold, face additional compliance obligations.

These include mechanisms involving:
automated detection
grievance officers
compliance officers

local points of contact

India-based compliance structures

periodic compliance reports

appeals processes

originator tracing in specified circumstances for messaging services.
So the rules are aimed not only at the person creating the deepfake.
They put a major compliance burden on the distribution network itself.
12. THE REAL STICK: SAFE HARBOUR
This is where it becomes serious for Meta, X, Google, Telegram and other intermediaries.
Section 79 of the IT Act provides intermediaries conditional protection from liability for third-party content.
But that protection depends upon complying with the law and prescribed due diligence.
The PIB release reiterates that failure to observe obligations under the IT Rules can result in the intermediary losing its Section 79 exemption, after which liability can arise under applicable law.

That makes the real equation:

Comply with due diligence → retain intermediary protection

Ignore statutory obligations → safe-harbour protection can be jeopardised

That is far more powerful than merely issuing a fine.

13. GOVERNMENT HAS BUILT A TAKEDOWN PIPELINE

There is now an increasingly integrated enforcement architecture:

Grievance Appellate Committees — GACs

Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre — I4C

SAHYOG Portal

National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal

police/cybercrime units

authorised State and Central Government agencies.

The SAHYOG system in particular enables centralised electronic communication of lawful content-removal notices to intermediaries.

14. INDIA IS ALSO BUILDING ITS OWN DEEPFAKE-DETECTION TECHNOLOGY

Under the IndiaAI Mission's Safe & Trusted AI pillar, government-backed work includes indigenous detection and governance technologies.
PIB identifies projects including:
Saakshya — multi-agent deepfake-detection framework developed by IIT Jodhpur and IIT Madras
AI Vishleshak — audio-visual forgery detection
IIT Kharagpur work on real-time voice deepfake detection.

So this is not purely a legal crackdown.

It is simultaneously a:

LEGAL + PLATFORM + TECHNOLOGICAL framework.

15. WHY THIS IS HAPPENING NOW

Generative AI has destroyed the old assumption that:
“Seeing is believing.”
Today one person can manufacture:

a politician announcing something he never said

a CEO apparently moving a stock

an Army officer issuing a fake warning

communal speeches

celebrity pornography

fake financial endorsements

fabricated battlefield footage

false evidence of violence
within minutes.
And the fake can reach millions before conventional fact-checking catches up.
Therefore the Indian approach is increasingly:
IDENTIFY → LABEL → DETECT → TRACE → REMOVE → PROSECUTE
rather than merely:
WAIT → RECEIVE COMPLAINT → INVESTIGATE.
THE BIG STORY FOR YOUR VIDEO

The headline isn't simply:

“Deepfakes must carry labels.”

The bigger story is that India is trying to change where responsibility lies.

Earlier, platforms could largely argue:

A user uploaded it; we are merely the intermediary.

The regulatory direction is increasingly:

If you operate the technology that generates, distributes or algorithmically amplifies synthetic content in India, you have duties to identify it, label it and respond rapidly when it becomes unlawful.

text:
A reproducible report gives the agent a failing signal and a finish line before it edits code.

“The button does not work” is not a coding-agent task. It is a symptom with the important bits missing. A GitHub issue template can force the report to contain observed behavior, expected behavior, reproduction steps and evidence before an agent turns uncertainty into a confident patch. That tiny structure saves more time than another clever prompt.

Make the template ask for the route or command, environment, exact steps, actual result, expected result and one useful artifact: error text, network response, log or screenshot. Add a field for the acceptance check. If the report says “checkout fails on the second click,” the finish line might be a browser test showing one order after two rapid submissions. “Page opens now” is not enough if the action still duplicates the order.

Give the agent the completed issue and tell it to reproduce the failure before editing. If it cannot reproduce it, it should return the attempted steps and observed result rather than silently fix a guess. Once the failing signal is real, ask for one hypothesis: what code path explains it, what observation would confirm it, and which smallest change would address it? Two failed hypotheses are a reason to inspect new evidence, not to keep changing files randomly.

The regression proof matters. A test that passes on the old behavior does not catch the bug. Ask for the red result before the patch and the green result after it, with exact commands and failures. Pick the cheapest test that crosses the broken boundary: unit for a pure function, integration for an authorization or database path, browser for a visible flow. If the environment cannot run the test, label that as unverified. A generated assertion is not a test result.

Keep the scope in the issue too. A password-reset bug is not permission to redesign authentication. State affected files or modules, non-goals and the condition that should make the agent stop. Ask for a compact final report: root cause, changed files, proof of reproduction, proof of fix and remaining uncertainty. A reviewer should be able to inspect the reasoning without replaying the whole agent conversation.

One honest note: templates are not a substitute for a product decision. If nobody knows the expected behavior, the agent cannot derive it from a screenshot. Route that question to the owner and keep the issue honest. Do not let “works as coded” become the acceptance criterion.

Pick the last bug an agent “fixed” without reproducing it. Turn that missing evidence into a required issue field. Your next repair should start with a fact, not a theory.

RAG vs. Graph RAG vs. Agentic RAG, clearly explained!

Standard RAG embeds documents into vectors and retrieves the most similar chunks via similarity search. For direct factual lookups, this works well.

But it breaks down when a query needs to connect facts spread across multiple documents. Similarity search retrieves individual chunks, not the relationships between them.

Graph RAG adds a knowledge graph layer on top.

→ During indexing, an LLM extracts entities and relationships from the documents.

→ During retrieval, the system traverses these connections instead of relying on embedding similarity alone.

This is what enables multi-hop queries.

Say a vector DB stores three facts about internal services:

↳ "The checkout service uses payments API."
↳ "The payments API runs on cluster-3."
↳ "Cluster-3 is scheduled for maintenance on Friday."

Someone asks: "Will the checkout service be affected by Friday's maintenance?"

Vector search can likely retrieve facts 1 and 3 because the query mentions "checkout service" and "Friday maintenance."

But it will miss fact 2, which connects the payments API to cluster-3.

That middle fact sits too far from the query in embedding space. It mentions neither "checkout" nor "maintenance," so it never makes it into the retrieved context.

A knowledge graph connects these as linked entities, and graph traversal finds the full path in one query.

Agentic RAG takes a different approach entirely.

Instead of a fixed retrieval pipeline, an LLM agent decides at query time which tools to invoke, which sources to query, and in what order.

Check the visual below to understand the three architectures thoroughly.

One thing to note here is that these three aren't levels of sophistication that you need to graduate through.

Instead, they solve different query types.

↳ Single-hop factual lookups → standard RAG
↳ Multi-hop relationship queries → Graph RAG
↳ Dynamic multi-source tasks with tool use → Agentic RAG

Once the right architecture is in place, the next leverage point is efficiency.

Most RAG architectures rely heavily on vector search, and that layer can be made 32x more memory-efficient using binary quantization.

text:
Tesla and Starlink have sought entry into India for years. Tesla was blocked by a 110% tariff and local manufacturing rules, while Starlink faced national security concerns.  

With Trump back, things have turned into a cakewalk for Elon. The EV import tariff dropped from 110% to 15%, opening doors for Tesla, and Starlink is also making inroads. This seems to be a result of diplomatic arm-twisting rather than mutual benefit.  

Still, I see a blessing in disguise wrt Tesla, especially for consumers. High tariffs are primarily imposed to help domestic manufacturers grow and make the country self-reliant. We gave a lot of space for Tatas, Marutis, Mahindras, etc., to grow, innovate, and dominate, even at the cost of Indian consumers paying to protect substandard products and keep out competitive alternatives.  

If local manufacturers still can't compete, so be it. The entry-level Tesla will cost less than 40 lakh and has much better specs, performance, range, and battery life than any domestic EV. Why should Indian consumers be denied that when even Chinese companies are selling cars in India?  

Starlink, however, is a potentially risky deal if not diligently regulated, primarily due to the threat to our digital sovereignty. If its per-consumer cost is lower than Jio's and Airtel's current rates, local ISPs will be wiped out, creating a duopoly. If Jio and Airtel shift much of their traffic to Starlink, we’d be at its mercy, Musk could cut off our internet, suppress counterviews, and ban users at will. He could also refuse to block content harmful to national security.

text:
To understand the midterms from the perspective of many long-time Collin County, Texas residents, you have to start with how fast the place changed 

In roughly 5-7 years, people who grew up here watched their schools, neighborhoods, and workplaces shift at a pace most of the country never sees 

I’ve lived in Allen since the 1970s 

Both of my sons graduated from Allen High School, one in 2016, the other in 2021 

The difference in those graduating classes was IMPOSSIBLE to miss 

The student body, the names on the program, the overall makeup of the school had changed dramatically in just 5 years 😳

That wasn’t my imagination 

What happened in Collin County over the last 5–7 years was unusually fast ⬇️

According to Census American Community Survey estimates:

• Collin County’s Asian Indian population nearly doubled in a recent five-year period, rising from roughly 81,000 to about 149,000 

• Frisco went from a low single-digit share of Indian residents in the early 2010s to nearly 20% of the city (~43,000 people) by the early-to-mid 2020’s 

• Plano has roughly 37,000, McKinney about 16,000, and Allen around 9,200 

This is one of the largest and fastest-growing Indian American communities IN THE USA 

A major driver has been the H-1B visa and Optional Practical Training (OPT) pipeline into tech, IT services, and finance 

The DFW area ranked among the TOP metros in the U.S. for new H-1B approvals in recent years…tens of thousands in a very short period of time 

Nationally, about 70% of H-1B visas go to workers from India 

Frisco and Plano have high volumes of filings, many from large Indian IT staffing and consulting firms that place workers at client sites, alongside U.S. companies that expanded or relocated here 

Texas leaders ACTIVELY RECRUITED those companies with incentives 💰💸💰

The jobs followed, and the federal visa system supplied a large share of the “skilled” workers 

The result showed up quickly in schools, neighborhoods, restaurants, grocery stores, temples, airports and workplaces 

My younger son graduated magna cum laude with a degree in data science last December and is still waiting tables 

My older son works at a large financial institution in the Northlake area 

When I visited the office, the large majority of workers were of Indian heritage 

These are NOT isolated anecdotes 

Entry-level competition in data and tech roles has been INTENSE, and long-time residents have watched the demographic composition of their towns change at a pace most places NEVER experience, EVER 

This is why many native Collin County residents say the place feels different and why local elections have shifted (hint: they mostly voted blue)

The change was real, measurable, and unusually, insanely RAPID 

We’re talking breakneck speed rapid 

Understanding the numbers and the mechanisms (corporate recruitment + H-1B/OPT concentration) helps explain what people have seen with their own eyes 👀 

If you’ve lived through this in Collin County or another fast-growing suburb, what has the pace of change looked like where you are?

I know many people have heard the stories, and those who don’t live here may think we have been exaggerating 

We’re not and we never were

Is there a “fix” for this? 

If so, how? 

Most of our friends and family live in Collin County, and most are discussing moving to another state, away from their native state 

Something they never thought they would think of doing, but they are definitely saying it now…and actively looking for a new place to live 

Texans have been sold out by leadership, and without the incentives Texas leadership offered, perhaps they would not have lost last week’s midterm elections 

Who knows? 

Yes, Texans are proud of our state, and have *mostly* been happy to be a “business friendly” state 

But, at what cost???

Statement : Meta told the Home Ministry it acted against 61,000 posts in the fortnight after Chalo Sansad. IFF calls for the record to be made public.

New Delhi, 13 November 2026

Meta has told the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), the cybercrime arm of the Ministry of Home Affairs, that it acted on more than 61,000 Facebook and Instagram posts it classified as violent and inciteful between 25 July and 7 August 2026, @ThePrintIndia reported on 12 November. That is about three posts a minute for 14 days. The period begins on the day the Education Minister resigned and the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) ended its protest at Jantar Mantar, five days after police used tear gas and a lathi charge against its Chalo Sansad march.

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the absence of any public account of this action. Meta disclosed the figure to the Home Ministry at a meeting on 21 August, and it became public only because the minutes were filed in the Supreme Court's suo motu proceedings on digital arrest scams.. In IFF's assessment, the minutes record direct pressure from the Ministry of Home Affairs on the content Meta carries.

As per the report in The Print a meeting was chaired by Rajesh Kumar, I4C's chief executive, and followed reviews by the Union Home Secretary, a parliamentary committee and a court-monitored committee on digital arrests. Its scope was wider than financial fraud. 

According to ThePrint, I4C sought an in-person briefing on "how the algorithm amplifies or suppresses specific content and viral accounts", an analysis of bot networks across prominent handles, and Meta's draft guidelines on deepfakes and re-uploaded content for review.
The minutes, as reported, do not state what the 61,000 posts concerned. It is not known which agency, if any, flagged them, or which law or company rule Meta applied. I4C itself did not accept aggregate figures when Meta cited 70 lakh pieces of content removed, it asked for examples with links. Users and the public are entitled to the same detail.

Complaints received by IFF show what was being restricted on Instagram as the period began. Here we are relying on our own inbound queries and requests for pro-bono help and legal assistance.

1) On 23 July, a story about the protests shared by a private account with 137 followers was made unavailable in India through what Instagram described as "an automated system implemented pursuant to legal requirements" under the IT Rules, 2021.

2) On 24 July, a reel by the journalist Ila Kazmi showing a Delhi Police facial recognition van scanning protesters at Jantar Mantar was withheld on a notice from "The Government of India / Law Enforcement under Section 79(3)(b)", which referred her to the Government of India for any questions. The Delhi High Court has directed the Home Ministry, the IT Ministry, the Delhi Police and Meta to produce the notice and will next hear the case on 17 November.

3) On 28 July, three days after the minister's resignation, Instagram withheld a video published on 15 June by the current-affairs page Unmutezone under the title "Why Modi Can't Ask Dharmendra Pradhan to Resign?". Its editor reported that a second video was blocked on 3 August.

Press reports describe similar restrictions. Newslaundry reported that an interview by the journalist Yaqut Ali with a former CJP spokesperson, posted on 26 July, was blocked in India within minutes, and that Facebook reels on the protests by the creator Jyoti Yadav, including an interview with AAP's Sanjay Singh, were restricted. It later reported restrictions on Instagram posts by Scroll and The Hindu about pellet-gun victims in Kashmir. None of this content is violent or inciteful, and Meta has not said whether it forms part of the figure.

The Home Ministry is involved at each stage from notices under Section 79(3)(b) reach platforms through the Sahyog portal, which I4C operates where close to 1.95 lakh blocking orders were issued to Instagram, Facebook and YouTube between March and July 2026, most of them through the portal, and Meta has integrated its systems with it so that flagged content can be restricted without human review. On 27 July the Delhi Police, which reports to the Home Ministry, was reported to have directed platforms to remove posts it considered offensive to the Prime Minister. Meta's transparency report lists violence and incitement among the categories that I4C refers to it. A ministry that operates this channel and also reviews Meta's enforcement figures and algorithm is supervising online speech.

We regret to state that the Supreme Court's own proceedings have provided an avenue for such censorship without sufficient checks and balances. In the suo motu digital arrest case, in which it directed intermediaries to place their proposals before I4C, and in the Just Rights for Children Alliance matters, in which it indicated that platforms may lose safe harbour, the Court has largely acted as a facilitator of executive action rather than as an adjudicator of its constitutional limits. The objectives of curbing fraud and protecting children are legitimate, but the supervision they have enabled now extends to lawful speech and results in censorship without legal authority.

These restrictions do not have a basis in law and often executive rulemaking is being used to circumvent the fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression. Section 79(3)(b) sets a condition for a platform's immunity and in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015), the Supreme Court confined it to court orders and government notifications within Article 19(2). The power to block lies in Section 69A, which requires written reasons, committee review and, following Tanul Thakur (2022), a copy of the order and a hearing for the author. Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules requires each intimation to state reasons, the provision, the unlawful act and the URL, and to be reviewed monthly by a Secretary-rank officer. These requirements cannot be met through an automated integration with a three-hour deadline, whatever share of the 61,000 posts came through Sahyog.

Further, we state that while it may constitute a category of harmful speech, "Violent and inciteful" is not a ground for state mandated censorship under Article 19(2). Shreya Singhal protects discussion and advocacy and permits restriction only at the stage of incitement; a video asking why a minister has not resigned is discussion. Nor is there any clear statutory basis for I4C to perform the function of review a platform's content guidelines or to ask which accounts its algorithm promotes.

Our demands

1) The Ministry of Home Affairs must publish the minutes of its meetings with Meta in 2026 and state how many of the 61,000 posts were flagged by I4C, the Delhi Police or any other agency through Sahyog.

2) Meta must publish a breakdown of the 61,000 posts by the rule or law applied, the action taken and the requesting authority, and give each affected user the notice on which it acted. Further monthly breakdowns with qualitative disclosure is necesary.

3) I4C must withdraw its requests to review Meta's draft guidelines and to be briefed on its algorithm. Oversight of this kind requires a law made by Parliament and may only be performed by an independent regulatory body with a clear mandate and objective.

4) The Union Government must publish the monthly Secretary-level reviews under Rule 3(1)(d) for July and August 2026.

5) Meta must end the automatic execution of government and police flags in India and provide human review, a reasoned notice and an opportunity to respond before any restriction.

Users whose posts or accounts were restricted in India in July or August 2026 may write to legal@internetfreedom.in with screenshots of each notice.

text:
Dear @raghav_chadha ,

I know you are doing very well in Parliament by raising small issues that were ignored by most Members of Parliament but have a bigger impact.

I am writing this post regarding an account lien and bank freeze by the Cyber Police of India.

In my case, the issue started when I received a message from my bank branch stating that my account had received a police notice of lien of 6000 rupees. I immediately went to my bank branch and asked them why my account had a lien of 6000 rupees. They followed some procedure and gave me a printout which contained the acknowledgement of my lien. One of the bank employees told me that I should contact the cyber police mentioned on the paper and provide them with the details of the 6000 rupees, such as where it came from and for what reason. However, they did not give me any specific reason why my bank account had received the lien.

Later, I checked my bank statement to find the details of the 6000 rupees transaction and noticed that my case was reported on 6 December 2025, and I had received a transaction of 6000 rupees on the same date. I remember that my neighbour had sent me this 6000 rupees and asked me to withdraw it from the ATM because he had an urgent situation as his mother was going to her village due to an emergency. As a friend, I withdrew the money and gave it to him.

Now I have all the proofs and details to explain to the police, so I emailed all the details to the Bangalore Cyber Cell or the police station where my notice was issued, as mentioned in the acknowledgement given by my bank. However, I did not receive any response. I then tried to contact the investigation officer mentioned in the report. I called several times, keeping a gap of five to six hours out of respect for his time and duties, as they may have many other responsibilities. I also sent him a message on WhatsApp, but there was still no response.

After four to five days, I called again, and this time he picked up the call. He was speaking in the local language, which I did not understand, as I am from Maharashtra and not familiar with the local language of Bangalore. I then started speaking in English, and he told me that I have to come to Bangalore and verify my documents. I explained that for 6000 rupees, it would not be beneficial for me to travel to Bangalore because transportation, food, and stay would cost more than 6000 rupees. He said that he does not know and that I have to come, otherwise he will not issue the No Objection Certificate, and then he ended the call.

This issue may look small, but similar issues are happening everywhere, and no one is noticing them. It feels like “Kare koi aur bhare koi.” Many innocent people face this issue, and it remains unresolved. Because of chain transactions that come into accounts, some people are unable to use their own money. If I travel, I will have to spend more than 6000 rupees to remove the lien. I believe this issue can be resolved through email or online verification, but the investigation officer denied it.

I am also tagging Pushpendra Sir @pushpendrakum and Bangalore Cyber Police @BlrCityPolice . If you could please look into this matter.

Thank you.
