🚨 ALLEGED CON ARTIST: Who is Louise Lucas? 

Let me share with you the backstory on a self-described "greedy" lawmaker who waged a war on merit, denigrating Asian American parents and families, and is now indicted for illegally selling marijuana and cheating to create "generational wealth" 

The text that indicts Virginia state Sen. Louise Lucas in a new Justice Department indictment announced by US Attorney General Todd Blanche and FBI Director Kash Patel against her for alleged money laundering is this one:

💰 “this is our last chance at generational wealth . . . I’ve got too old to not be greedy.”

The words she allegedly later said: 
💰 “I got to get the license and I got to get the money rolling because I want — I want to make generation, create some generational wealth.”

Lucas is an important window into the choices that everyone faces: whether to advance in life through merit or through cheating. 

Read our coverage of the indictment here: 

'FOR PEOPLE WHO LOOK LIKE ME'
I know the day that I learned the name of Virginia state Sen. Louise Lucas: Feb. 18, 2021. 

WATCH the video I've shared her to see Lucas in action.

She was supporting Virginia state Sen. Scott Surovell and other Democratic lawmakers as they waged a wider battle to remove merit-based admissions to America's former No. 1 high school, Thomas Jefferson High School for Science and Technology, and other governor schools. Their bill: HB 2305.

There were some 20 mostly immigrant parents waiting to speak in the online waiting room: parents from India, China and elsewhere, who saw merit as the only path they have to realizing the American Dream and maybe if they were lucky creating "generational wealth."

Lucas wouldn't let the parents speak. I was watching the debate from the waiting room. My son was attending the school at the time, and I was writing about the efforts of parents to challenge the new admissions policy, eliminating the merit admissions test, as racist. 

A federal judge Conrad Hilton later supported the parents and the Coalition for TJ and called the new admissions policy "patently unconsitutional" and racist.

The ruling was overturned on appeal and the US Supreme Court wouldn't hear the appeal but is now set to hear a similar case from Montgomery County, Md.

Then-state Sen. Chap Petersen was opposing that effort as an effort to target the school's mostly Asian American student population. 

As Petersen spoke about TJ, he noted, “Its population is 80 percent minority.”

Lucas, who is black, interrupted him and said, “Sen. Petersen, for people who look like me, I would appreciate it if you would put a better definition to minority, because I know you’re not talking about people who look like me, so could you please, please be more specific?”

Petersen, whose wife is Korean American woman, said: “The population is about 70 percent Asian.”

Then he added: “People who look like my kids. My kids.” 

Lucas responded: "Mm-hmm."

The war on merit succeeded and TJHSST has plummeted in academic standards and national rankings and is now the FORMER No. 1 high school. Current Virginia Lt. Governor Ghazala Hashmi demonized "parents" and alleged they were racist and supported Lucas and Surovell. 

When Lucas lost the vote, she said: "We will overcome one day."

🔗 This is the full 2018 debate for anyone who wants to see Lucas and her war on merit: https://t.co/w7iGZqXnnW

FAST FORWARD: "GREED" vs. MERIT
Federal prosecutors allege one Lucas, used her political office as part of a years-long operation to sell marijuana, launder the proceeds — and ultimately turn Virginia’s legalization of recreational marijuana into what she allegedly called “generational wealth," not through merit but by allegedly cheating the system.

The 45-page federal indictment names names: 
❌ Louise Lucas
❌ Her daughter Lisa Lucas-Burke
❌ Her daughter Theresa Lucas-Lamb
❌ Her grandson Ryan Eichelberger
❌ Businessman Prince Albert William Hudson III 
❌ Businessman Carlton Upton Jr.
❌ Businesswoman Tameka Johnson

Prosecutors allege the “Lucas Enterprise” operated from at least 2019 -- two years before the debate on merit -- and pursued two intertwined objectives: 
❌ Distributing marijuana
❌ Using Lucas’ political influence to shape Virginia marijuana policy and obtain valuable recreational licenses

Here is the extraordinary chronology prosecutors laid out, in their own words. 

RISE TO POWER
Lucas was elected to the Virginia Senate in 1991 and rose to become chair of the powerful Senate Finance and Appropriations Committee and Senate President Pro Tempore.

According to the indictment, her family operated The Cannabis Outlet in Portsmouth.

💰 Her daughter Lisa Lucas-Burke allegedly handled business affairs and attended meetings.
💰 Her daughter Theresa Lucas-Lamb allegedly managed the store.
💰 Grandson Ryan Eichelberger allegedly worked in its day-to-day operations.

Prosecutors say Lucas was explicitly warned.

After a senior law-enforcement officer was hired in 2022, the indictment says he warned Lucas that selling marijuana was illegal and “was going to get her in trouble one day.”

At another meeting, the officer allegedly asked why, “given that she was a state senator and a wealthy woman,” she would engage in criminal behavior.

According to prosecutors, Lucas didn't answer.

By then, prosecutors allege marijuana was already moving through the family business.

2022: 'FREEDOM IS DOPE'
In early 2022, prosecutors say an alleged supplier identified ICC #1 contributed $15,000 to the 420ish Unity Festival, partly organized by Lucas.

The receipt allegedly described the payment as:

“Freedom is Dope.”

Then, on April 19, 2022, Lucas and daughter Lisa Lucas-Burke allegedly met ICC #1 at Lucas’ office.

The indictment says that between June and July 2022, an alleged supplier identified as ICC #1 delivered between THREE AND FIVE POUNDS of marijuana to The Cannabis Outlet.

Lucas allegedly paid between $3,500 and $4,000 IN CASH.

'VIRGINIA FREEDOM LIFE'
According to the indictment, Lucas asked ICC #1 whether he was a member of law enforcement before discussing marijuana prices.

That same day, daughter Lucas-Burke allegedly wrote a $6,600 check to ICC #1 from Virginia Freedom Life.

It bounced.

Lucas allegedly replaced it with another $6,600 check from Backyard Entertainment.

By fall 2022, prosecutors allege the business was operating at scale.

Between fall 2022 and early 2023, ICC #2 allegedly sold The Cannabis Outlet “multi-pound quantities of marijuana totaling approximately 100 pounds” for $100,000-$150,000.

Prosecutors say Lucas, through daughter Theresa Lucas-Lamb, paid $52,000 in checks and the remainder IN CASH.

Then came the texts.

'THE LUCAS LADIES'
On Oct. 3, 2022, prosecutors say Lucas texted the alleged supplier:

“Good morning … this is to confirm the time for our meeting at the store today. I am so excited and looking forward to seeing you”

And:

“we (The Lucas Ladies) love doing business with you”

'I'M GOING TO NEED MORE FLOWER'
Daughter Theresa Lucas-Lamb allegedly texted with the supplier about the mechanics of marijuana sales.

One message described packaging and selling “half ounces (14)” and “ounces (28).”

Another allegedly said:

“you can keep going on the blend if you can’t keep up with sativa and indica.”

Days later:

“Good morning. I’m going to need more flower.”

The money trail continued.

The indictment lists payment after payment from The Cannabis Outlet to Prince Albert William Hudson III, whom prosecutors describe as a marijuana supplier.

💰 December 2023: more than $21,000.
💰 January 2024: more than $26,000.
💰 February: more than $29,000.
💰 March: $129,000.
💰 April: $132,000.
💰 May: $125,000.
💰 June: $123,000.
💰 July: more than $79,000.
💰 August: $91,000.
💰 September: $67,000.

And investigators weren't merely watching.

💰 On Oct. 4, 2024, and Oct. 18, 2024, the indictment says law enforcement made CONTROLLED PURCHASES of marijuana from The Cannabis Outlet.

More controlled buys followed.

💰 On May 5, 2025, an undercover officer allegedly bought 10.2 grams of marijuana from The CBD Shoppe.

💰 By 2025, prosecutors allege payments continued flowing to Hudson and another alleged supplier, ICC #1.

The indictment records tens of thousands of dollars month after month.

Meanwhile, daughter Theresa Lucas-Lamb allegedly received a series of $2,500 payments from an Agri-Carter account controlled by Hudson.

Then investigators intercepted a shipment.

On Aug. 13, 2025, Norfolk police seized SEVEN POUNDS OF MARIJUANA allegedly shipped to High-N-Wellness in Norfolk.

According to prosecutors, payments and marijuana transactions nevertheless continued.

By October 2025, law enforcement was buying directly from The Cannabis Outlet again.

💰 Oct. 23, 2025: controlled purchase of ½ ounce.
💰 Oct. 31, 2025: controlled purchase of one ounce.

During that transaction, prosecutors say Eichelberger told the undercover officer another load of “product” was due Nov. 3.

'THE ELECTION' 
Then came a text prosecutors put directly into the indictment.

On Nov. 15, 2025, Lucas allegedly wrote about “the election” and told ICC #2:

“you know I will be carrying the legislation as the Chief Co-patron.”

She allegedly proposed sitting down to discuss “how about we begin with you sending at least a good faith payment of the money you owe me…”

'LIST OF STUFF FOR YOU TO TRY'
In January 2026, prosecutors say the operation moved directly into Lucas’ legislative office.

Grandson Ryan Eichelberger allegedly began texting businesswoman Tameka Johnson asking for “a lil have a list of stuff for you to try & get for next time.”

Then: “can you get the COAs for the flower and other products?”

💰 On Jan. 30, 2026, according to prosecutors, Lucas asked ICC #2 to come to her office at the Capitol complex in Richmond.

💰 There, the indictment says Lucas provided “partial repayment” of money ICC #2 had paid for an interest in Mama’s Chicken, LLC.

💰 Then Lucas allegedly asked ICC #2 to provide marijuana “samples.”

💰 The next day, Jan. 31, 2026, prosecutors say Lucas and ICC #2 met AGAIN — this time at her legislative office in Portsmouth.

Lucas allegedly called in daughter Lisa Lucas-Burke and grandson Ryan Eichelberger.

They discussed sources of marijuana.

When Eichelberger asked whether the cannabis was hemp, prosecutors say ICC #2 replied:

“[I]t’s not hemp, it’s THC.”

'GET GENERATIONAL WEALTH'
Then prosecutors allege Lucas explained the endgame.

After the conversation, Lucas and ICC #2 allegedly continued discussing marijuana and marijuana licensing.

According to the indictment, Lucas said obtaining a license was a way for her to:

“get generational wealth and this is my last chance.”

The alleged undercover operation kept going.

💰 Feb. 3, 2026: ICC #1 allegedly arrived at The Cannabis Outlet with “a large bag” from his vehicle and took it inside.

💰 Feb. 5, 2026: controlled purchase of 69.5 grams from The CBD Shoppe.

💰 Same day: controlled purchase of 116 grams from High-N-Wellness.

💰 On Feb. 9, 2026, prosecutors say Lucas called ICC #2 and discussed the recreational-marijuana legislation pending in the General Assembly.

The indictment quotes Lucas:

“this is our last chance at generational wealth . . . I’ve got too old to not be greedy.”

Two days later, law enforcement allegedly observed ICC #2 throwing a white trash bag into a dumpster.

Investigators recovered it.

The indictment says the bag contained marijuana packaging bearing “the odor of marijuana.”

March 2026: prosecutors allege the political and business sides increasingly converged.

Lucas allegedly told grandson Eichelberger and businesswoman Tameka Johnson to find additional marijuana sources.

Then, prosecutors say, Lucas telephoned another Virginia legislator and explained why she needed a marijuana license.

The alleged quote is stunning:

“I got to get the license and I got to get the money rolling because I want — I want to make generation, create some generational wealth.”

She allegedly continued:

“I need to be covered under his (UPTON’s) um, hemp license.”

On March 11, 2026. prosecutors say Lucas participated in another call with Virginia legislators and daughter Lisa Lucas-Burke about recreational marijuana licenses.

Lucas allegedly said:

“we trying to disqualify somebody [UCC #2] until he pays me back my money.”

March 31, 2026: Businessman Carlton Upton Jr. allegedly met Lucas at her Portsmouth office.

According to the indictment, Upton told Lucas:

“I only got five licenses, but you know what I mean, you first, so I need to talk to you before I make any decisions that affect you.”

💰 April 23, 2026: prosecutors say Lucas called a member of the Virginia Cannabis Control Authority and asked whether there was anything the official could do for her.

💰 According to the indictment, Lucas said she needed “to invest in something that — that can help me generate some uh, generational wealth for my family.”

Then came the raids.

💰 May 6, 2026: Federal search warrant at The Cannabis Outlet — marijuana recovered.
💰 Federal search warrant at The CBD Shoppe — marijuana recovered.
💰 Federal search warrant at Hudson’s Exotic World in Danville — marijuana recovered.
💰 July 10, 2026: Law enforcement returned to The Cannabis Outlet for another controlled purchase.
💰 Agents bought two strains labeled “Sativa” and “Indica.” According to the indictment: Both tested positive for marijuana.

The grand jury ultimately charged an alleged racketeering conspiracy involving Lucas, daughter Lisa Lucas-Burke, businessman Prince Albert William Hudson III, grandson Ryan Eichelberger, daughter Theresa Lucas-Lamb and businessman Carlton Upton Jr.

Prosecutors say the alleged enterprise sought to obtain and illegally distribute marijuana AND procure “generational wealth” for its members.

The indictment goes further.

Prosecutors allege the enterprise used business entities to disguise marijuana proceeds and used Lucas’ political influence “to insulate the Lucas Enterprise from state law enforcement actions.”

They also allege her influence was used to pursue marijuana licenses that could financially benefit the enterprise.

Prosecutors describe Lucas as the alleged “leader of the enterprise.”

They accuse her of approving and directing criminal activities, arranging marijuana acquisition and distribution, supervising laundering of marijuana proceeds and using her political influence in an effort to shape Virginia legislation for herself and her family.

The indictment contains EIGHT COUNTS, including allegations involving:

❌ Racketeering conspiracy
❌ Conspiracy to distribute and possess with intent to distribute marijuana
❌ Money laundering conspiracy
❌ Honest-services fraud conspiracy
❌ Maintaining drug-involved premises
❌ Possession of a firearm in furtherance of a drug-trafficking crime
❌ Wire fraud

The charges vary by defendant.

One of the most consequential allegations isn't simply that marijuana was illegally sold.

Prosecutors allege Lucas used her elected office to advance the financial interests of herself, her family and associates as Virginia debated creation of a potentially lucrative recreational marijuana market.

The honest-services count alleges a scheme to deprive Virginians of Lucas’ “intangible right” to her honest services.

The indictment alleges Lucas invested money with ICC #2 in an entity positioned to benefit from marijuana licensing, did not report that interest on required Statements of Economic Interests, and later demanded a partial $100,000 repayment while continuing to work to direct a license to ICC #2.

These are allegations. An indictment is not proof of guilt, and every defendant is presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty. 

That's the position that Sen. Surovell, the lawmaker who pushed the legislation to remove merit from Virginia's No. 1 high school, is taking as he stands by her in support against the indictments.

The government has now laid out, in extraordinary detail, its theory of how an alleged marijuana business, a family network, money and political power converged over years.

And prosecutors repeatedly return to the phrases they attribute to Lucas herself: creating "generational wealth" by being "greedy."

I hope the telling of this story will give you a wider window into why this case captures not only the crossroads that a politician faces of success through merit or through cheating but also the questions that a nation faces: to go down the path that this lawmaker allegedy supported of shortcuts and dishonor or to choose a path of honor, merit and hard work. 

In 2021, Lucas silenced parents who believed in merit and hard work. 

Today, in 2026, she is facing serious charges for violating "honest-services" laws, money laundering, wire fraud and racketeering.

In which path do you believe?

The defense challenged this, wondering where Mr Andrew Mubiru has ever seen a person convicted on confidential information they can’t challenge. 

Over the defense’s protests, the Uganda Police Forensic Services Director essentially invited the court presided over by Justice Isaac Muwata to substitute scientific rigor with blind trust. 

You might recall that the same Mr Andrew Mubiru back when he was working as an analyst at the Directorate of Government Analytical Laboratory (DGAL), was found by the Court of Appeal of Uganda in the Kato Kajubi case, to have tested a non-existent sample and reported results as if he had actually tested a real sample. (See frame 2) 

Below is a transcript of that September 2024 cross-examination. 

Mr Elison Karuhanga of Kampala Associated Advocates was the defense attorney doing the cross examination. 

They’re discussing results from a comparative analysis of DNA material found on different items gotten as exhibits from the Katanga household and from Mrs Katanga in IHK (hospital) where she was receiving medical care for what a prosecution expert categorized as life threatening injuries sustained from being beaten by her now deceased husband, Late Henry Katanga. 

The reference DNA samples are; a buccal swab from Mrs Molly Katanga which is reasonably expected to only have her DNA and a swab taken from Mr Henry Katanga during postmortem plus other members of the household. (You can see full video in the quoted tweet)
 
EK: Now, it then tells us if it was a mixture or a single source, correct? 

(Note: a single source profile is when the available DNA is from one contributor/person. A mixture is when the results show there’s at least 2 people.)

AM: This is a qualitative approach which is able to show us that we are matching a single source.

EK: No, no, no, no. Does it tell us if it is a mixture or a single source?

(Note: This point is important because as it was later to be revealed, the state analyzed several DNA samples, got results as per software they used, then state analysts edited them to reflect a picture that’s different than what the system had showed. They then presented these edited results to court as DNA evidence against Mrs Katanga. In some cases, according to Mr Mubiru, some samples had at least 2 people’s DNA, they scrapped off the other person (or people) and reported it as being only Mrs Katanga’s DNA. This was never disclosed to the court or the defense until when Mr Mubiru was caught during cross examination; part of which you can find in the already referenced video)

AM: This is a qualitative arrangement, but it looks as though there are some loci which indicate additional alleles.

(Just for the non-medical science folks, here’s a basic explanation of what it is the defense and the key prosecution witness were arguing over:

 At each location in our DNA (called a locus, plural loci), we each carry two versions, called “alleles”: one from our mother and one from our father. In the test used here, an allele is named by a number, such as 12 or 15. The lab's software reads peaks on a chart called an electropherogram and labels them as alleles ("allele calls"), and an analyst then reviews those labels. Because one person can have at most two alleles at any locus, finding a third or fourth points to DNA from more than one person. When Mr Mubiru testified that there appeared to be additional alleles, he was acknowledging material beyond the two that matched Mrs Katanga's reference sample (12 and 15 at that locus). He told court he treated the extra peaks as "stutter," a machine artifact, and edited them out at review, then reported the sample as coming from a single person. The defence argues those peaks were real DNA from someone else, which would mean evidence that might point elsewhere was left out of the report. According to the defense’s cross-examination of Mr Mubiru, it wasn’t just done for one sample, it was done for several samples and the original data hidden because “it’s confidential”)

EK: Hold on, hold on. Does it tell us if it is (a single source or a mixture)? Look, look, there's a word called mixture. Do you see the word called mixture?
AM: Yes.
EK: Now, for the sample 682Y23S004, which is (a swab from) Molly Katanga's mouth, does it say yes or no?
AM stammers: "The mixture called this, the system….”

EK: Does it say yes or no?
AM: It says yes. 

(Note: AM saying the swab from Mrs Katanga’s mouth showed a mixed DNA profile would be a bit strange. 

Mr Karuhanga is having none of that. He insists that Mr Mubiru should read his own report and tell court what he sees)

EK: No, it says no. Read. 682Y23S004. Mixture; what's the answer to that?

AM: No. (AM eventually admits that it’s a single source profile and not a mixture)

EK: So what about the bed sheet? Is the bed sheet a mixture or a single source profile?
AM: For S008 it says yes. It says it's a mixture.
EK: Yes. And you reported it as a single source?
AM: Yes, and there's a reason why
EK: Let's first record that it says it's a mixture and you recorded it as a single source.
AM: Yes.

(It’s at this point that the wheels started coming off of the state’s DNA evidence juggernaut)

EK: Now, before you even get to the reason, I want you to go to the table at page 45….a color table. 
EK: So, can you find for us the loci D8, can you find for us the loci D8, D8S1179, on the top here?
EK: So that is the... that's the eighth one, yeah?
 
EK to Judge Muwata: If you count this here, my Lord, after sample ID, we have one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, which is the D8S1179.
AM: Yes.

EK: Yeah? Now, what alleles do you have from your table recorded there?
AM: 12 and 15.

(Note: These are Mrs Katanga’s alleles. Basically think about them as part of a unique DNA serial number)

EK: So at location D8S1179, you record two alleles, 12 and 15.
AM: 12 and 15.
EK: 12 and 15 means mother, father. Two alleles, one person, correct?
AM: That's what we were able to record for that specimen.
EK: Two alleles for one person.
AM: This is an evidential material, so you cannot just say mother, father.
EK: Yeah, yeah, yeah. But what it means is she gets one number from the mother and one number from the father.

(Note: what EK was saying is also what the science says; you inherit one from your mother and one your father)

AM: My Lord, I repeat, that is misleading. This is a piece of evidence which was found at the scene. 
EK: No, no, no. What I mean, those numbers, one number comes from a father, one number comes from a mother...
AM: For a single source profile. For a single source profile of a known contributor.

EK: So you would say that this is a single source profile because there are two alleles.
AM: It's a single source profile, but remember this is...
EK: Because there are two alleles.
AM: Yes.

EK: And if there are three, those become two people.
AM: That is a mixed profile…because what we usually say is “at least two people”, if there are three (alleles)

EK: Now let's go back to our match statistic. And we go to the same allele, D8S1179. That is on page eight.

EK: But the table has only two numbers, 12 and 15, indicating it's a single source profile.
EK to AM: Now go to the table in the match report.
EK: Not that one. This table, or the report itself, which is Annex 3, page 8. 
Judge Muwata: Yes

EK to AM: Now, on the number 682Y23S008, at that location, how many alleles are there?
AM: aaah, the allele call has 12, 15 and 16.
EK: So there's a new number, 16.
AM: That's one of the allele calls which we…
EK: Yes, so it has 12, 15 and 16.

EK to Judge Muwata: That's my Lord here, D8S1179….it is the eighth... It's actually the eighth number from the top. This is at page 8.
Judge Muwata: Yes….

EK to Judge Muwata: And then the location which starts D8S1179. So for the sample for Molly Katanga's mouth, it has 12 and 15, indicating it is one person. For the sample for the bedsheet, it has 12, 15 and 16.
Judge Muwata: It has 12 and what?
EK: It has 12 and 15, that is for 004. And then for the bed sheet, it has 12, 15 and 16. 
Judge Muwata: 12, 15 and 16
EK continues: Indicating two people. 
AM: At least two people, if you look at it from a qualitative aspect.
EK to AM: So when you write in your report that you recovered a single person (profile), that is incorrect?
AM: That is still not accurate, my Lord. 
EK: The report is not accurate?
AM: The report takes into consideration all the analysis I did. This is a qualitative analysis. I also do a quantitative analysis.

EK: So now, let's go slow. When you put in your table that at this location you found only two alleles, is that part of your table false?
AM: No, it is accurate.

EK squeezes AM further: So did you find allele number 16?
AM: Allele number 16 was later reviewed under quantitative arrangement and excluded on grounds of stutter.
EK: Now, it was excluded on grounds of stutter. So can you go to it in the electropherogram?

(Note: The EPG is like the master result form for DNA analysis. Before qualitatively and quantitatively cleaning results, the electropherogram must have them reflected)

AM: It was later reviewed under... It was excluded on the grounds of stutter.

Judge Muwata inquires into how allele 16 was excluded. Mr Mubiru insists “it was excluded because it was deemed to be stutter from peak number 15”. 

(Note: Think earthquake and then the tremors after. They can’t be reported as an earthquake. That’s how stutter is; earthquake happens and then you have post-quake tremors. THe defense essentially says that in a series of independent earthquakes, Mr Muburi ignored entire earthquakes and instead picked the one he liked and called the rest tremors. 

To relate it to DNA, on an electropherogram (EPG), “stutter” are those peaks that don’t meet the detection threshold. They may be looked at as background noise and at times, it’s best to remove them. But also, in the same vein, one can just remove peaks they find inconvenient to a pre-conceived outcome and blame it on stutter. At times, they can raise the detection threshold to a level much higher than the system is set at just to remove these inconvenient peaks. Mr Mubiru, as we’ve reported previously, was later found through cross examination by the defense and through the testimony of defense DNA expert, Ms Lynne Hingley, that he did both of these “scientific tricks”. He shifted the detection threshold from the system validated 70 to 300. He just didn’t change this on the electropherogram and Ms Lynne Hingley caught it and showed it to current presiding Judge Rosette Comfort Kania. As Mr Karuhanga told another prosecution witness in this same case, “the science caught Mr Andrew Mubiru”. But I digress…)

EK to AM: Let's go to the electropherogram. You testified the only audit which we have are these, and now you are introducing things which are not in your report. But let us move…
EK: I think page 21.
Judge Muwata: Page 21, what are you referring to?
EK: We are looking at the electropherogram, and also here, we don't have the 16, correct?
AM inquires as to the page
EK: Page 21 (of the EPG)…for sample S008

EK: We are looking at the second, at the second D8. There is a row which starts Y-indel, then Amel, then D8.

EK to AM: So for that one, the 16 is not there, correct?
AM: Yah, the 16 is not there.
EK: Do you see the stutter of the 16?
AM: aaaah, errr…I can see there is something there, but...
EK: Where? There are two peaks.

Judge Muwata: What is this one?
EK to Judge Muwata: This is the electropherogram, my Lord. This document is the electropherogram for the bed sheet recovered from Molly Katanga. The witness said that there was stutter. When you look at it quantitatively, there was a peak which he reviewed and looked at as stutter when he went through a qualitative analysis. So I'm asking him to show us the stutter. Now, my Lord, if you look, D8 has only 12 and 15. They are simply two peaks.

EK to AM: So can you confirm that you cannot see any stutter when you look at 12 and 15?
AM: A loud silence….he says nothing.
 
Judge Muwata to AM: Is that so?
AM: There's a small… peak there, which is…errr…which usually comes as a result of stutter. For example, on D16 you can...
EK: No, no, no. We're on D8! We're not on D16. Give us an example from D8!
AM: Pregnant silence…no answer.
 
EK to Judge Muwata: My Lord, D8 is just the second... the sample name 682. The first row is this Alpha One, then the second one. Then there's something called Y-indel, there's something called Amel, then there's D8S1179. Below that there are two green peaks. Below the green peaks there are numbers. There's a box which says 12 and there's another box which says 15. Judge Muwata: Yes….
EK to Judge Muwata: So the witness says there's also a box which has stutter, and now I'm just asking him to show us the stutter on the electropherogram.

AM finally walks back his earlier claim and admits the stutter he claimed was there was not there: My Lord, it's not displayed on the electropherogram.
EK: It is not displayed. So it's not there. It's not displayed on the electropherogram. The stutter is not there.
AM: It’s not displayed on the electropherogram

Judge Muwata: The stutter…?
EK: The stutter is not there

Judge Muwata then asks EK whether they’ll bring a technical person to explain all this to him
EK: No, my Lord he’s here. The technical man is here, my Lord…(as he points to Mr Andrew Mubiru)
EK continues: And what he's telling us is that his match report has an allele that doesn't exist on the electropherogram. Is that correct?
AM: My Lord, after a quantitative review, the stutter peak was removed.
EK: So this is an edited electropherogram.
AM: My Lord, these electropherograms are continuously reviewed for purposes of our work. 

(Note: He didn’t say which part of their work includes reporting results different than what the system offers)

EK: Let's just get this straight. What has been brought before this court is edited. This particular electropherogram is edited even from the moment we start doing the analysis.
EK: Thank you. First stop there, let’s first record this.

Judge Muwata: How was it edited? 
EK: Is another word for edited, Doctored?
AM: No.

Judge Muwata: It was edited, how, Sir? 
AM: My Lord, in the course of analysis, the electroherogram has artifacts and those artifacts are filtered by the system upon a quantitative review. 

(Note: Here, Mr Mubiru tells Judge Muwata that the editing or “review” is done by the system) 

EK: So if they (the artifacts) are filtered, how are they ending up in our match report?
AM: Yah, because when you are doing a qualitative review, the system uploads some information, then you have a chance to look at what it has developed, and then you give it a new metric for quantitative review.
EK: And do you have... let's just get that. When you are doing a what? I didn't hear you. When you are doing a...?
AM: Quantitative review.

EK: So there is a quantitative review and a qualitative review. So before this court, what is there?
AM: We give you the answers regarding the quantitative review.
EK: So we don't have enough information before this court?
AM: You have also the qualitative review, which you have already demonstrated to court.
EK: It's demonstrating that you're editing things…
AM: No, you do a qualitative review and then after that you do a quantitative review.

EK: So there's a review which we don't have?
AM: You already have it in the report.
EK: So show me the stutter. Where is it? Show me the report.
AM: You have already showed court. My Lord, he has already showed you the 16. 
EK: Where’s it?
AM: It is in the qualitative report.
EK: Which is where? Show us. Take us to a page and say, "on this page we removed the 16 because there is a qualitative stutter."
AM: My Lord, counsel has already showed you where we uploaded [on] the system; he has already showed you where the stutter is. And after that, it will be a quantitative review.

(Note: EK asked AM to show court the stutter and he eventually said it wasn’t there. It’s unclear what he meant by saying Counsel had showed court the stutter at 16)

EK: No, no, no. This (the EPG) comes first. Doesn't this come first? You testified that the only way we can audit you is by looking at this, the table and the match. I have given you just one sample. I have many I'm going through, so I want us to be clear on the answers.
AM: That's why I explained to court, my Lord, that the qualitative review allows us to go back to the electropherogram in order to understand what a qualitative review you’ve done (sic) so that now you can do a quantitative review. 

(It’s unclear as to what the pre-eminent Uganda Police DNA Forensics expert meant by that)

EK: So, and it is your evidence that this electropherogram you provided to this court is edited?
AM: The electropherogram automatically has to be looked in by the analyst.
EK: So it's edited by you?
AM: We all have to look at it.
EK: So you edited it?
AM: Yes, I edited it from the moment we….look at the artifacts….

(Note: Here, Mr Mubiru switches from saying it’s the system that edited to its them (the analysts) that edited)

EK: I think... let's first, hold on. Let's first record that you edited the evidence.
AM: My Lord, it's not (editing) per se. It's called a review. That's the technical term.

EK: And nowhere do you give us the review. Can you confirm that we asked you for internal validation studies and you hid them?
AM: My Lord, the internal validation studies are studies which are done to confirm that the assay is fit for purpose.

EK: Can you confirm that we asked you for the original data and you hid it?
AM: My Lord, the original data is available, but it's confidential.

An exasperated EK then says: My Lord!! Who have you ever had being convicted on confidential information? You're here to give evidence in court. You're supposed to tell the court everything. You don't have secrets. This is not your DNA, it's hers (Mrs Katanga’s). Why are you hiding it from her? It is yours which is confidential. 

AM cleverly skirts that point and instead goes on to talk about validation studies: My Lord, the validation studies are not done on the DNA of any suspect or person.

EK isn’t falling for it. He asks again about the original data that pertains to Mrs Katanga’s DNA. That’s the data that Mr Mubiru called “confidential”: “The data... not about... I’m talking about the original data. That there’s no data before this court to confirm this evidence.”

Judge Muwata: The original data is confidential?
EK: Yes

Mr Mubiru again skirts that point and goes back to talking about validation studies: The validation studies are done….

EK cuts him off: The data, I’m talking about the data!

Assistant DPP Samali Wakooli to EK: Nooo…

AM: Yes, the validation studies…
EK: Okay, the validation studies? 
AM: the validation studies are done using another set of data and that data is confidential because we utilize a different set of specimens.

EK goes back to the point Mr Mubiru has been trying to avoid: And what about data... What about Molly's DNA?

Judge Muwata asks AM if he wants to answer. AM keeps quiet then Judge Muwata says, “anyway, it’s on record, if you don’t want…”

EK: No, my Lord, I think he says they (validation studies) are done using another set of data. 
Judge Muwata: Is that what you wanted to say?
AM: My Lord the validation studies are done at a point when we do installation of the equipment. They’re done in concert with the manufacturer of the equipment and the people who are authorized to run these validation studies. And actually they’re not per se validation, they’re verification studies within the system. 

He didn’t speak to Mrs Katanga’s original DNA data and Mr Karuhanga didn’t push him any further. Instead, he moved to another sample 

EK: Okay, I want you to look at another sample on the electropherogram first….TO BE CONTINUED.

UgandaVsMollyKatanga resumes on 26th November 2026 for mention.

ICYMI: The Day The Director of Forensic Services in Uganda Police, ACP Andrew Mubiru Told Court That The Results Before Court Were Edited and Not The Actual Results The Analysis System Produced. 

The defense called them “doctored”, he called them “edited” and said there was a reason for the editing, which he never provided. 

He also declined to provide the original form of the results, edit history or validation studies for independent verification as well; calling them “confidential”. 

I’m not making this up, read on for details.

I’ll explain in a three part series but first, the broad details;

In September 2024, during cross-examination by defence attorney Mr Elison Karuhanga, the Director of Forensics at @PoliceUg, Mr Andrew Kizimula Mubiru, was asked about the DNA electropherograms (EPGs) he had placed before court.

He said he was the analyst and he edited them. When asked for the originals, he said they were “confidential”. You might recall from our earlier reports that Mr Mubiru later denied being the analyst

Why this matters:

EPGs are computer generated graphs that display raw data produced during DNA separation and analysis. Reading them against a reference sample tells you how many people’s DNA is present, whose it is etc. Editing some peaks out cleverly hides this information.

The state's DNA report says a bed sheet recovered from Mrs Molly Katanga carried a single person's DNA profile, hers.

But the system's own match report, which Mr Mubiru attached as Annex 3, said otherwise. It flagged the bed sheet as a MIXTURE. At two DNA markers (D8S1179 and D7), the system recorded three alleles. Three alleles means at least two people.

The electropherograms before court showed only two alleles.

Asked where the third peak went, Mr Mubiru said it was a "stutter", a small artefact of the DNA copying process, and that he had removed it on review.

Mr Karuhanga asked him to show the stutter on the electropherogram.

He said: "It's not displayed”

EK: "So this is an edited electropherogram."

AM: "Yes, I edited."

He later conceded that, according to the system, the bed sheet "indicates a mixture… more than one person's DNA on it."

And when asked for the raw data and internal validation studies that would let anyone check his call? "The original data is available, but it's confidential."

Note: Removing stutter can be legitimate. Labs do it. But a stutter and a second person's DNA can look EXACTLY alike on a graph. The decision to call a peak "stutter" can turn a two-person mixture into a single-source profile. In a murder trial, that can be the whole case.

Mr Mubiru just invited court to not check him; but take his word for it; a courtroom version of “trust me bro”. 

He edited the graphs, set thresholds that didn’t match his own testimony, then held the raw data as "confidential". 

He invited court to ditch the science and instead trust him.

The Defense’s View

Mr Karuhanga called the police forensics lab “a kitchen that cooks results”.

Fast forward to July 2026;

Defense DNA expert Ms Lynne Hingley (DW4) told court:

1-Mr Mubiru said they used a threshold of 300 RFUs to remove noise (edit). The state's own software report shows 70. (See here: https://t.co/Hh3TUGnrAM)

2-A negative control contained DNA from at least 2 people, "a gross contamination event."

3-One gun sample with 4 contributors was modelled as if it had 3. The model then failed validation checks 7 times.

4-Even with perfect results, "the DNA result itself does not help address in any way who fired that gun."

On the issue of who was the analyst anyway? 

Mr Mubiru answered that. Well, sort of….

On different days, he described himself as the analyst, the lead examiner, the supervisor, "supervisor, not examiner," and the reviewer. 

He also told court the logged-in users were ASP Barnabas Haririmana and SP Lillian Mutesi, not himself. (See here: https://t.co/X40FfMb160)

You can find the cross-examination link here: https://t.co/sqSO9eIQyw

Delhi Police asks X to take down IFF's account and posts. IFF will challenge the notices in court unless they are withdrawn.

The Delhi Police has asked X to remove the Internet Freedom Foundation's account, six of its posts, the accounts of SFLC and @geoblockedindia, and posts by 16 other users, on the ground that they defame the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh. The posts document and comment on a legal notice sent in the RSS's name to IFF, SFLC and @geoblockedindia, which demanded that the three stop criticising and documenting government blocking orders. IFF received copies of the two police notices from X on the morning of 3 November 2026.
IFF calls on the Delhi Police to withdraw both notices. If they are not withdrawn, IFF will challenge them in court.

What has happened

On 29 October 2026 at 9:54 PM, IFF, SFLC and the operator of @geoblockedindia received a two-page "legal notice" said to be issued on behalf of the RSS. It asked the three to stop opposing the government's blocking directions, stop documenting restricted content, stop posting details of geo-blocked posts, and confirm in writing within seven days that they would comply. It was signed by an unnamed "Authorised Signatory". Several RSS office-bearers have since said on X that the notice is not authentic. IFF replied to the notice, wrote to the RSS at its official address asking whether it had authorised it, and published both the notice and its reply on 30 October.

On 31 October 2026 at 8:06 PM, the Special Commissioner of Police (Crime), Delhi Police, filed an "Illegal Content Report" with X (reference LD-321926). It listed two posts: IFF's post of 30 October on the notice, and SFLC post of the same day. The stated reason was that the posts are "defamatory towards the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh under Section 356 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023". The boxes for "safety/security", "defamation" and "other" were ticked. The fields for the nature of the court order and court order details were left empty. The desired action was "Remove/withhold content".

On 1 November 2026, a second notice arrived in the RSS's name. It said the matter had been handed to the Akhil Bharatiya Adhivakta Parishad, that complaints had been filed in several states, and that requests had been made to block IFF's X account and suspend the organisations. The Delhi Police had made its first request to X the previous evening. IFF did not know this until X told it on 3 November.

On 2 November 2026 at 8:51 AM, the Special Commissioner of Police (Crime) filed a second notice with X (reference LD-322956). It lists 40 URLs. Thirty-seven are posts. Three are the entire accounts of @internetfreedom, @SFLCin and @geoblockedindia. This time the boxes for "Hate speech", "defamation", "safety/security", "enforcement of court order" and "other" were all ticked. The court order fields were again left empty. The stated reason reads: "The posts constitute defamation and illegal content under Section 356 BNS. Under Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021, read with Section 79(3)(b) IT Act, lawful notices require action within 3 hours."

The 16 other users are @ProdctiveUseful, @PanjwaniManoj, @jidge_, @RatanSharda55, @baxiabhishek, @SchrdingersDbag, @ashleshbiradar, @seemay, @NasirHussainINC, @Being_creat_ive, @AjoyDharmavaram, @othlaw, @_ananyaaa, @AimPoojaind, @incorigibleBhai and @rraoind. Their posts, as far as IFF can tell, comment on the notice or on the notice about it.

X forwarded both notice to IFF on 3 November 2026, at 8:47 AM and 10:03 AM, saying it was doing so "in the interest of transparency" and that IFF may wish to seek legal counsel and challenge the request in court. X's emails do not say that it has acted on the requests. The Delhi Police has not written to IFF, and no court has been approached, as far as the reports disclose. SFLC and @geoblockedindia have separately reported notifications from X about requests from the Uttar Pradesh Police, the Telangana Police and the Delhi Police's Cyber Crime unit, one of them against the whole of the @geoblockedindia account.

IFF's position

IFF condemns this legal action. A police force has made itself the enforcement arm of a private legal notice whose authenticity the organisation it names has not confirmed, and whose demand was that three organisations stop documenting censorship. The notices would deliver exactly what the notice asked for as they would also remove the accounts of the three groups in India that keep public records of what is blocked, and of who ordered it.

The posts in question are about a legal notice sent to us. They quote it, criticise how it was drafted, and say that we will carry on with our work. A person who receives a threat is entitled to publish it and answer it and that is not defamation of the sender. 

In the three weeks before the first notice, IFF assisted 86 people whose accounts were suspended or whose posts were withheld in India. SFLC's Free Speech Tracker recorded about 268 content restrictions and 83 account restrictions in the first 29 days of October. @geoblockedindia publishes the orders behind such blocks when platforms disclose them. None of this is unlawful. Documenting censorship and challenging it in court is what the Constitution expects of citizens.
IFF will not delete the posts. If the Delhi Police does not withdraw the notices, we will challenge them in court.

Why the reports are unlawful

Defamation is not a police matter. Section 356 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 is a non-cognizable and bailable offence. Under Section 222 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, no court can take cognizance of it except on a complaint by the person aggrieved. 

Under Section 174 of the BNSS, the police cannot investigate a non-cognizable offence without an order of a Magistrate. The Special Commissioner of Police (Crime) is not the person aggrieved. The notices disclose no complaint by the RSS and no order of any Magistrate. Whether a statement is defamatory is for a court to decide after hearing its author, with the defences of truth, fair comment and good faith available to that author. 

In Subramanian Swamy v. Union of India, (2016) 7 SCC 221, the Supreme Court upheld criminal defamation on the strength of these safeguards. A police officer who asks a platform to remove speech as defamatory has decided the question himself, without a complainant, a court or a hearing.

The posts are protected comment. Exceptions 1 to 3 to Section 356(1) protect the truth published for the public good, opinion on the public conduct of public servants, and opinion on the conduct of any person touching a public question. The posts publish a notice that was sent to us and give our opinion of it. The RSS, if it sent the notice, chose to enter a public question. If it did not, the posts defame no one.

Further, Section 79(3)(b) and Rule 3(1)(d) do not permit this. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court read down Section 79(3)(b) so that an intermediary acquires "actual knowledge" only through a court order, or a notification from the appropriate government or its agency that unlawful acts relatable to Article 19(2) are being committed. The court said that it would be difficult for intermediaries to judge the legitimacy of the millions of requests they receive, and that the burden must not be placed on them. Rule 3(1)(d), as amended in November 2025 and February 2026, now requires the intimation to come from an officer not below the rank of Joint Secretary or Deputy Inspector General, to be reasoned, and to specify the legal basis and the nature of the unlawful act, subject to a monthly review by a Secretary-level officer. The three-hour window the notice invokes applies to a lawful order that meets these conditions. A web form that ticks "hate speech" and "enforcement of court order" while leaving the court order fields blank, and that gives one sentence of reasons for 40 URLs, is not such an order.

The notices by the Delhi Police are disproportionate. They seek to remove three accounts in their entirety, with years of posts, over six, four and eleven posts respectively. They sweep in 16 third parties whose only connection is that they commented on a public controversy. In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637, the Supreme Court held that any restriction on speech must be necessary, proportionate and the least restrictive measure available, and that orders restricting speech must be published and reasoned. Removing an organisation's entire account for criticising a legal notice fails each of these tests.

The effect is to silence documentation of censorship and providing legal aid to Indian internet users. The accounts named are those that record blocking orders in India. The notice asked them to stop. A takedown request that accomplishes the demand of an anonymous private notice is not law enforcement. It is the use of state power for a private end, which Article 14 forbids.

Our demands

1. To the Delhi Police: Withdraw reports LD-321926 and LD-322956 and confirm the withdrawal in writing to X and to IFF. 

2. To the Delhi Police: Disclose the complaint on which the Special Commissioner of Police (Crime) acted, the authority under which the reports were filed, and whether any order of a Magistrate under Section 174 BNSS exists. Disclose every request made to any platform in this matter, including those made by the Cyber Crime unit against @geoblockedindia.

3. To X: Do not act on the reports. If any content is withheld in India, tell the affected user before acting, give them the full request, and name the legal basis. Publish both reports to the Lumen database, as the reporting form itself contemplates.

4. To the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology and the Ministry of Home Affairs: Have the Secretary-level review required by Rule 3(1)(d) examine these intimations, and tell police forces that Rule 3(1)(d) is not a remedy for defamation, which the law reserves to the person aggrieved and to the courts.

5. To the RSS: State publicly whether it authorised either notice or any complaint to the police. If it did not, say so to the Delhi Police.

If the notices are not withdrawn, IFF will challenge them in court. We will continue to document blocking orders, to publish them, and to provide legal assistance to anyone whose account or post is withheld in India. Nothing in these notices changes that.

text:
I have my twitter back. 

It took me 6 days, a cyber police complaint and a legal notice to twitter to recover my account. 

If you got a DM from me last week asking you to vote for me for a podcast, that was not me. Please don't click it & If you already did, please change your password ASAP.

Here's what happened:

→I received a late night DM from a friend to vote on a podcast which redirected me to a a login page that looked right, and I typed in my password (classic)

→The attacker logged in and changed my 2FA within minutes & I was locked out of my account. (I still don't understand how my email and phone number were changed. Neither my email nor my phone was compromised.)

→Then he used account to DM followers a fake "vote for me" link. Each person who clicks becomes the next account sending it. That is how these spread.

What didn't work:

→ I filed X's hacked account form within the hour. Less than two hours later, the reply came: X could not verify me as the account owner. Their suggestion was to create a new account. Once 2FA is changed, the automated system treats the attacker as the real owner.

→ So I went to the Grievance Officer. Under the IT Rules, 2021, X must appoint a Resident Grievance Officer in India. He has no email address. X does not accept legal notices by email. 

The only options are a web form or post to their physical office.

Here's what worked:

→First, a cyber complaint on https://t.co/Uzds8BObDW (or call 1930).

→Second, a legal notice to the Grievance Officer. Under the IT Rules, impersonation complaints must be acted on within 24 hours.

→Third, the same notice sent by registered post, and to every X email address I could find.

The notice put X on record. It set out the ticket number, the phishing link, and the cyber complaint number. It showed proof of ownership: the registered email, the phone number, and the Premium subscription paid from my card. It ended with a clear ask and a deadline.

Six days after the hack, I was back in.

If this happens to you:
• Act within hours
• File X's hacked account form from your registered email and be persistent (this is important)
• File at https://t.co/Uzds8BObDW and keep the acknowledgement
• Notice to the Grievance Officer via the https://t.co/YkDfcMQwzE form and by post

Statement : The removal of BitChat from the India App Store is unconstitutional. Section 69A permits the blocking of unlawful information, not of a messenger for working during internet shutdowns.

New Delhi, 3 October 2026

An Apple App Review notice published today by Jack Dorsey on X records that BitChat has been removed from the India App Store "per demand from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology", issued under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, on the ground that the application "includes content that is illegal in India". The notice adds that BitChat's TestFlight builds are no longer available for testing in India. It does not identify the content said to be illegal or the ground under Section 69A invoked. The blocking order has not been published. The Internet Freedom Foundation condemns the order and calls for its immediate publication and withdrawal.

BitChat relays end-to-end encrypted messages between nearby phones over Bluetooth mesh. It has no servers and hosts no content of its own. What travels through it is the private speech of its users, so the claim that the application "includes" illegal content is incoherent. The State's actual objection stands recorded in the notices the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre issued on 23 July 2026 to GitHub, Google and Apple against BitChat, Briar and Bridgefy which stated that such applications work even during internet shutdowns and hamper lawful interception, attribution and traceability. Those notices, issued under Section 79(3)(b) were reportedly withdrawn after public disclosure. The same end has now been pursued through Section 69A. The objection is to capability of an application, not to content it transmits. A citizen's ability to speak to another citizen while the State has switched the internet off is not a ground of restriction under Section 69A or Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

Section 69A survived constitutional scrutiny in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) because of its safeguards which included the need for a reasoned, recorded order, committee review, and a hearing to the originator under Rule 8 of the Blocking Rules, 2009, which the Delhi High Court enforced in Tanul Thakur v. Union of India (2022). Further, Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) requires that orders restricting fundamental rights be published and adopt the least restrictive measure. However, it appears in this instance, each safeguard has been evaded. A secret order blocking an entire application, rather than any identified unlawful information, is the most restrictive and disproprotionate measure available. Further, the confidentiality claimed under Rule 16 cannot defeat the right to challenge an order, and the constitutionality of this blocking regime is itself pending consideration before the Supreme Court.

While removal from the App Store does not delete BitChat from phones, it stops new downloads and security updates, leaving existing users on unpatched versions, and it ends security testing in India through TestFlight. During the Jantar Mantar protests, when mobile internet was suspended and jammers were deployed, Bluetooth mesh messaging was a channel of last resort through which young people coordinated their safety. To our knowledge, Apple has removed BitChat on a government's demand in only one other country. This is in China, in April this year.

Our demands

1. MeitY must publish the blocking order, the ground invoked and the record of the committee's proceedings, and serve the developers with a copy and an opportunity of hearing.

2. The direction must be withdrawn. Any specific unlawful use must be met with targeted proceedings under due process, not the removal of a communications tool for everyone.

3. Apple must disclose the demand in its transparency reporting and notify its users in India, and must state whether parallel directions have been received in respect of other app stores.

4. The secrecy of the blocking regime must end. The Blocking Rules, 2009 should be amended to require publication of orders and notice to originators, without awaiting the outcome of the pending constitutional challenge.

The Internet Freedom Foundation will file applications under the Right to Information Act seeking a copy of the order, and stands ready to assist the developers and affected users in India.

Dear @raghav_chadha ,

I know you are doing very well in Parliament by raising small issues that were ignored by most Members of Parliament but have a bigger impact.

I am writing this post regarding an account lien and bank freeze by the Cyber Police of India.

In my case, the issue started when I received a message from my bank branch stating that my account had received a police notice of lien of 6000 rupees. I immediately went to my bank branch and asked them why my account had a lien of 6000 rupees. They followed some procedure and gave me a printout which contained the acknowledgement of my lien. One of the bank employees told me that I should contact the cyber police mentioned on the paper and provide them with the details of the 6000 rupees, such as where it came from and for what reason. However, they did not give me any specific reason why my bank account had received the lien.

Later, I checked my bank statement to find the details of the 6000 rupees transaction and noticed that my case was reported on 6 December 2025, and I had received a transaction of 6000 rupees on the same date. I remember that my neighbour had sent me this 6000 rupees and asked me to withdraw it from the ATM because he had an urgent situation as his mother was going to her village due to an emergency. As a friend, I withdrew the money and gave it to him.

Now I have all the proofs and details to explain to the police, so I emailed all the details to the Bangalore Cyber Cell or the police station where my notice was issued, as mentioned in the acknowledgement given by my bank. However, I did not receive any response. I then tried to contact the investigation officer mentioned in the report. I called several times, keeping a gap of five to six hours out of respect for his time and duties, as they may have many other responsibilities. I also sent him a message on WhatsApp, but there was still no response.

After four to five days, I called again, and this time he picked up the call. He was speaking in the local language, which I did not understand, as I am from Maharashtra and not familiar with the local language of Bangalore. I then started speaking in English, and he told me that I have to come to Bangalore and verify my documents. I explained that for 6000 rupees, it would not be beneficial for me to travel to Bangalore because transportation, food, and stay would cost more than 6000 rupees. He said that he does not know and that I have to come, otherwise he will not issue the No Objection Certificate, and then he ended the call.

This issue may look small, but similar issues are happening everywhere, and no one is noticing them. It feels like “Kare koi aur bhare koi.” Many innocent people face this issue, and it remains unresolved. Because of chain transactions that come into accounts, some people are unable to use their own money. If I travel, I will have to spend more than 6000 rupees to remove the lien. I believe this issue can be resolved through email or online verification, but the investigation officer denied it.

I am also tagging Pushpendra Sir @pushpendrakum and Bangalore Cyber Police @BlrCityPolice . If you could please look into this matter.

Thank you.

Dear Shri Amit Shah Ji,

Namaste.

I write as a concerned citizen to bring to your urgent attention the direct role of foreign VPN services in enabling heinous crimes against children, women, and acts of terrorism—crimes that are actively bypassing existing Indian laws. Section 70B(6) of the Information Technology Act, 2000, via directions issued on 28 April 2022, imposes a mandatory 5-year logging requirement on VPN providers.

Despite the mandatory 5-year logging requirement imposed on VPN providers under these directions, major foreign VPNs—NordVPN, ExpressVPN, Surfshark, ProtonVPN, Mullvad, and others—have openly refused compliance by removing physical servers from India and routing traffic through virtual IPs abroad. This deliberate non-cooperation has turned these services into safe havens for criminals and terrorists operating in and targeting India.

For example, the global money laundering and terrorist financing watchdog, Financial Action Task Force (FATF), reported on July 8, 2025, that the accused in two recent terror attacks in India—the Gorakhnath Temple attack in Uttar Pradesh on April 3, 2022, and the Pulwama suicide-bomb attack in February 2019, which killed 40 CRPF personnel—used online payment services, e-commerce platforms, and Virtual Private Networks (VPNs).

Terrorism (VPN-Enabled Plots/Propaganda)

Foreign VPN Use in Crimes in India (2020–2025)

Here are 10 news reports from 2020–2025 detailing cases where foreign VPNs (or non-compliant international VPN services) were used to commit or facilitate crimes against children (CSAM/pornography), women (sextortion/cyberstalking), terrorism/national security threats, or other serious offenses (ransomware/fraud/drug trafficking) in India. Each includes a brief summary, crime type, and primary source link.

During COVID-19 lockdown, ICPF report noted a 100% surge in child pornography searches (5M/month across 100 cities), with users employing foreign VPNs to bypass India's CSAM bans.
Crime: Child exploitation → Times of India

City police arrested 30 in 38 child pornography cases based on cyber intel; offenders used international VPNs to browse dark net/paid sites, prompted by NCCRP tips.

Sir, the pattern is undeniable:

- They enable child exploitation, pornography, violence against women, radicalization, drug trafficking and terrorist activity.

Requested Immediate Possible Actions for Consideration:

1. Publish a National Registry of Compliant VPNs
Direct CERT-In and MeitY to publish and maintain a public registry of VPN providers that have demonstrated compliance with the 28 April 2022 CERT-In Directions issued under the Information Technology Act, 2000.
Requirement: Five-year data logging, real-time incident reporting, and appointment of an Indian-resident nodal officer.
Purpose: Establish transparency and a verifiable compliance benchmark for enforcement.

2. Delist and Prohibit Operation of Non-Compliant Foreign VPNs
Instruct Apple, Google, and all Indian ISPs to immediately delist and block all non-compliant foreign VPNs, including NordVPN, ProtonVPN, ExpressVPN, Surfshark, and Mullvad, that have refused to adhere to the 2022 CERT-In Directions.
Action: To be taken under the blocking powers of the Information Technology Act and its associated Intermediary Guidelines.
Purpose: Prevent evasion of Indian jurisdiction and close routes for offenders hiding behind virtual foreign IPs.

3. Block Associated Payment Channels
Direct the Reserve Bank of India and all licensed payment aggregators and card networks such as PayU, Razorpay, Visa, and Mastercard to suspend or block subscription transactions to banned or non-compliant VPN providers.
Purpose: Cut off domestic funding and revenue flows sustaining illegal VPN operations.

4. Mandate Exclusive Use of CERT-In Certified VPNs
Require, through regulatory notification, that only VPNs, whether Indian or foreign, that obtain CERT-In certification be permitted to operate in India.
All VPNs advertising Indian IP services must maintain logging infrastructure within Indian jurisdiction and comply with lawful requests from enforcement agencies.
Purpose: Ensure traceability and lawful accountability of all VPN activity associated with Indian IP addresses.

5. Criminalise Intentional Use for Concealment During Offences
Propose suitable amendments or notifications under the Information Technology Act and India’s relevant penal codes to criminalise the intentional use of banned or non-compliant VPNs for concealing identity during the commission of cognisable offences involving child sexual abuse material, terrorism, radicalisation, or financial fraud.
Purpose: Target deliberate misuse while preserving lawful privacy.

6. Strengthen Traceability and Cooperation
Mandate that every VPN provider operating in India:
(a) Designate a resident nodal officer;
(b) Retain subscriber and metadata for five years; and
(c) Respond to law enforcement requests within seventy-two hours, as required by the CERT-In Directions of 2022.
Purpose: Guarantee swift investigatory access while preserving due process.

7. Establish a National Honeypot and Canarytoken Programme
Authorise CERT-In and the National Cybercrime Threat Analytics Unit to deploy a nationwide honeypot and Canarytoken framework, as validated in peer-reviewed research, to trace VPN-enabled crimes involving child sexual abuse material, sextortion, ransomware, and terror financing.
Ensure judicial oversight, privacy protection, and certified chain of custody for admissibility of digital evidence.
Purpose: Build indigenous technical capability to unmask offenders using VPN anonymity.

8. Strengthen International Coordination and FATF Alignment
Direct NIA, CBI, and MHA’s Cyber Coordination Centre to:
(a) Formalise fast-track cooperation with FBI, Europol, and Interpol under Mutual Legal Assistance Treaties; and
(b) Report VPN-linked money-laundering or terror-financing incidents to the Financial Action Task Force in conformity with its Comprehensive Update on Terrorist Financing Risks dated 8 July 2025.
Purpose: Integrate India’s enforcement with global counter-terror and cybercrime frameworks.

9. Institute Annual CERT-In Audit and Enforcement Schedule
Require annual audits of VPN providers’ compliance and publish audit summaries for public accountability.
Providers failing to comply beyond sixty days after notice should face permanent blocking and notifications to RBI, DoT, and MeitY for coordinated enforcement.
Purpose: Ensure continuous oversight and eliminate recurring non-compliance.

10. Issue a Public Advisory and Compliance Deadline
Issue a national advisory within thirty days, notifying all VPN providers of a sixty-day compliance window.
After the deadline, non-compliant entities should face delisting, domain blocking, and payment interdiction without exception.
Purpose: Provide procedural fairness before enforcement action begins.

India must not remain a playground for foreign tools that shield sexual predators, criminals and terrorists. The Ministry of Home Affairs has already acted strictly—forcing Apple and Google to delist 6+ non-compliant VPNs in January 2025. It is time to complete the job.

text:
https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 strongly objects to the takedown requests targeting its X handle and posts documenting instances of online censorship in India. 
 
On 3 November 2026 at 3:18 AM and 4:33 AM, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 received an email from X’s Legal Department informing us that it had received takedown requests from the Delhi Police concerning 42 URLs. These include the handles of https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2, @internetfreedom, @geoblockedindia, and posts from the said organisations and other users. A separate notification identified five (5) URLs concerning https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2’s X account and our posts.

The requests relate to posts discussing legal notices received by https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2, IFF and @geoblockedindia from an advocate purportedly acting on behalf of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS). They also include posts by users who commented on or reshared these posts, as well as other posts by @geoblockedindia documenting instances of digital censorship.

Chain of Events

1. On 29 October 2026, when https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2, IFF and @geoblockedindia (collectively “Organisations”) received a legal notice from an advocate purportedly acting on behalf of the RSS. The notice took objection to https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2's Free Speech Tracker, which documents instances of censorship and online content restrictions and account takedowns in India. https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 and IFF raised concerns about the authenticity of the notice, which did not carry an official letterhead or identify an authorised signatory.

2. On 1 November 2026, the Organisations received another notice from the same advocate. This notice stated that the matter had been transferred to the RSS's legal and advocacy wing, the Akhil Bharatiya Adhivakta Parishad, and referred to complaints allegedly filed in different states.

3. On the same day, X informed https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 that it had received a request from the “Indian Police” alleging that a post discussing the legal notice violated Indian law. However, this notification did not identify the requesting law enforcement agency, statutory provisions invoked, or provide a copy of the underlying order or request. The post remains accessible on X at the time of writing.

4. On 3 November 2026, X communicated further directions from Delhi Police covering 42 URLs, including the URL for https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2’s account itself. In the attached notices, the first notice refers to Section 356 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023 which deals with the offence of criminal defamation as the legal basis. The second notice refers to Section 356 of BNS and Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, read with Rule 3(1)(b) of the Information Technology Rules 2021, which deal with intermediary liability and due diligence of intermediaries as the legal basis. The grounds cited for the takedown requests concerning https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2’s X handle and posts include hate speech, defamation of RSS, and safety/security.

Takedown requests targeting https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2's handle threaten its public service work

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2's X handle is an important public-facing channel through which it disseminates the organisation's ongoing work to the general public. It is through https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 social media handles that users who face digital rights violation and online harms reach out to us for pro bono legal services. Through the handle we publish legal and policy analysis, document instances of censorship, raise awareness about digital rights violations, and communicate such information with the public including journalists, researchers, civil society organisations among others. It also serves as a channel for sharing developments concerning internet shutdowns, content restrictions, account takedowns and other violations of digital rights and for providing important assistance, through RightsLine, to citizens facing online harms ranging from gender based violence and harassment  to cyberfraud. 

A direction seeking the takedown of an organisation’s entire account, rather than addressing specific content through a transparent and legally established process, would have consequences far beyond the posts that have been identified. It would also deprive the public of an established and credible source of information on digital rights and the exercise of fundamental freedoms online.

The request to restrict https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2’s entire X handle, rather than identifying and seeking the removal of specific allegedly unlawful content does not meet the necessity and proportionality standards. The right to freedom of expression under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution extends to disseminate information, circulate ideas and reach an audience.  Restrictions on fundamental freedoms must not be arbitrary or excessive and must not go beyond what is necessary to achieve their legitimate objective (Chintaman Rao v. State of Madhya Pradesh, AIR 1951 SC 118). Any restriction on an organisation's established channel of communication must therefore be assessed in light of its wider impact on the organisation's ability to exercise its rights and the public's corresponding right to receive information.

Further, the reliance on Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, 2000, read with Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021, raises questions to whether intermediary liability provisions are being used as an independent mechanism for restricting online speech, potentially bypassing the procedural safeguards prescribed under Section 69A of the IT Act and the Blocking Rules, 2009. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court read down Section 79(3)(b), clarifying that an intermediary's obligation to remove or disable access to content must arise from a court order or notification by the appropriate government or its agency, and that such orders or notifications must strictly conform to the grounds enumerated under Article 19(2) of the Constitution. Section 79(3)(b), which forms part of the intermediary safe-harbour framework, cannot be treated as an unrestricted or independent source of blocking power or used to circumvent the safeguards governing restrictions on online information.

It is also pertinent to note that https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 in Software Freedom Law Center, India v. State of NCT of Delhi & Ors, W.P.(C) 7650/2025 has also challenged the constitutional legality of the notification issued by Lieutenant Governor (LG) which empowers the Delhi Police to issue takedown orders for removal of online content from social media. The matter is currently pending in the Delhi High Court.

Documenting censorship is not facilitating circumvention

The Free Speech Tracker is an initiative to document instances of censorship in India. Its purpose is to make censorship visible, identify patterns in content moderation and provide the public with information about restrictions affecting online expression.

Documenting a restriction does not amount to endorsing the restricted content, facilitating access to it or encouraging circumvention of the law. Over the last few months, we have seen an unprecedented number of online content restrictions happening in India, and in the absence of adequate transparency from the government and platforms about the nature, extent and legal basis of these restrictions, we wanted to document these instances in a manner that is informative to the general public. Freedom of expression encompasses not only the right to publish and disseminate information but also the right to question restrictions on speech, seek accountability and scrutinise decisions affecting public discourse.

Independent civil society organisations like ours play an important role in documenting these developments and ensuring that restrictions on online expression do not go unnoticed. Such takedown requests risk creating a chilling effect on public-interest advocacy and may discourage individuals from discussing or questioning instances of censorship.

Irregularities in notice received

The first notice received by https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 from X, pertains to this post. The notice states that the content in question is being reported on the grounds of ‘safety/security; defamation; and other’. Furthermore, the notice states that the post is “defamatory towards the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh under the Section 356 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS).” Criminal defamation under Section 356 of the BNS, 2023, is a non-cognizable offence and therefore, requires a court order for the police to initiate action.

The second notice received, pertains to a list of 42 posts and accounts. The notice states that the content in question is being reported on the grounds of “Hate speech; safety/security; defamation; enforcement of court order; and other’. The posts published by https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 did not contain any defamatory statements or allegations against RSS, as it was purely factual reporting based on information relating to the notice received by the Organisations on 29 October 2026.

Furthermore, criminal defamation is a non-cognizable offence which requires a court order for the police to initiate action. The Delhi Police is not empowered to issue a content takedown order for such offence via the Sahyog Portal in the absence of such an order. While the notice mentions enforcement of a court order as one of the grounds, no such court order is cited or made available in the notice. Additionally, the notice does not identify a legal basis or statutory provision for the offences of hate speech or safety/security. The notice also relies on Rule 3(1)(d) of the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 read with Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, 2000 and states that action must be taken by X within 3 hours.

Therefore, in light of the above, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 condemns the takedown request issued by the Delhi Police and maintains that they are unlawful, disproportionate and violative of the fundamental rights to freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a). https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 calls upon the Delhi Police and the concerned authorities to immediately withdraw these requests. If there exists any relevant court order directing the removal of the content, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 calls upon the Delhi Police to provide copies of said order to the Organisations (https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2, IFF, and @geoblockedindia) posthaste. 

We stand in solidarity with all individuals and organisations affected by these takedown requests and reaffirm our commitment to defending their right to speak, document and question restrictions on online expression. Transparency, accountability and access to remedies must remain central to any process that seeks to restrict online expression.
